bills.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act
bills.official_title: An act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14.
bills.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill permanently extends the 2017 Trump-era tax cuts, adds new deductions for tips and overtime pay, tightens eligibility for SNAP food assistance and Medicaid, funds more than $109 billion in new border security and immigration enforcement, and rescinds most of the Inflation Reduction Act's climate and clean energy spending. It also raises the federal debt ceiling by $5 trillion to finance the combined cost.
bills.brief: Makes the 2017 Trump tax cuts permanent, creates tip and overtime deductions, funds a $109 billion border buildup, imposes Medicaid work requirements, and terminates most IRA clean energy programs.

top_lines.headline: Tax Cuts Made Permanent
subs: Individual tax rates of 10%–37% made permanent; estate tax exemption increased to $15 million
Standard deduction raised to $15,750 for single filers and $31,500 for joint filers (inflation-adjusted)
Child tax credit increased to $2,200 per qualifying child; SALT deduction cap raised to $40,000 through 2029, reverting to $10,000 in 2030

top_lines.headline: New Deductions for Workers
subs: Up to $25,000 deduction for qualified tip income (2025–2028)
Up to $12,500 deduction for overtime compensation (2025–2028)
Up to $10,000 deduction for passenger vehicle loan interest (2025–2028)
New "Trump accounts" — tax-advantaged IRAs for under-18s with a one-time $1,000 government deposit for births in 2025–2028

top_lines.headline: Border Security and Immigration Enforcement
subs: $46 billion to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for physical barriers, technology, and access roads through FY2029
$45 billion to ICE for expanded detention capacity through FY2029
$29 billion to ICE for hiring, transportation, and removal operations through FY2029
New immigration court fees: $100 for asylum applications, $1,000 for parolees, $5,000 for individuals apprehended between ports of entry

top_lines.headline: SNAP and Medicaid Changes
subs: SNAP work requirements extended to adults up to age 65 (from 55); parents of children 14 and older must also meet requirements
States required to share 5–15% of SNAP benefit costs starting FY2028 based on payment error rate; federal admin cost share cut from 50% to 25%
Medicaid expansion enrollees must complete 80 hours per month of work or community service beginning in FY2027
Medicaid eligibility redetermined every six months for expansion population (previously annual)

top_lines.headline: Defense and Security Investments
subs: $29.2 billion for the shipbuilding industrial base and naval shipbuilding (FY2025)
$24.4 billion for space-based missile intercept and ground-based missile defense (FY2025)
$25.4 billion for hypersonic, cruise, and anti-ship missiles (FY2025)
$14.7 billion for nuclear forces and production, including B-21 bomber expansion (FY2025)

top_lines.headline: Clean Energy Tax Credits Terminated
subs: Consumer EV tax credit (up to $7,500) and used EV credit (up to $4,000) terminated October 1, 2025
Home energy efficiency credit (up to $3,200) and residential clean energy credit terminated 2026
Wind and solar clean electricity production and investment credits terminated for new projects after 2027
Clean hydrogen production credit terminated for projects starting construction after 2027

top_lines.headline: Energy Production and IRA Rescissions
subs: Oil and gas royalty rates reduced on federal lands; onshore lease sales resumed in specified states
ANWR: at least 4 lease sales within 10 years; NPR-A: at least 5 lease sales within 10 years
$389 million for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; repeals Biden-era drawdown requirement
Rescinds unobligated IRA funds for Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, school air quality, climate justice grants, and dozens of other EPA climate programs

top_lines.headline: Student Loans and Education
subs: Graduate PLUS loans eliminated for new loans on or after July 1, 2026
Aggregate student loan caps: $100,000 for graduate students, $200,000 for professional students, $257,500 lifetime limit
All current income-based repayment plans terminated for new loans; borrowers limited to standard plan or new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP)
$10.5 billion in additional Pell Grant funding for FY2026; new Workforce Pell Grants for 150–600 clock-hour programs

top_lines.headline: Debt Limit and Other Provisions
subs: Statutory debt limit increased by $5 trillion
$24.5 billion to the Coast Guard for vessels, aircraft, and shore infrastructure through FY2029
$12.52 billion for FAA facilities modernization including $4.75 billion for telecom infrastructure and $3 billion for radar replacement
$9.995 billion to NASA for Moon and Mars missions and International Space Station deorbit

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on July 4, 2025, as Public Law 119-21. The bill passed both chambers along party lines under the Senate's reconciliation procedure, which requires only a simple majority and cannot be filibustered. Republicans held the House and Senate majority and used reconciliation to bypass the Senate's 60-vote threshold.

sections.label: Title I — Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

items.main: Tightens SNAP eligibility and cost structure: work requirements extended to age 65, state cost-sharing of 5–15% beginning FY2028, and federal administrative cost share cut from 50% to 25%.
items.detail: SNAP state cost-sharing is calculated on a sliding scale based on the state's payment error rate — states below 6% pay nothing; states at 10% or above pay 15%. States may no longer request waivers of the three-month SNAP time limit based on insufficient job availability. SNAP-ED nutrition education grants are eliminated. SNAP eligibility is removed for certain legally present immigrants, including domestic violence and trafficking survivors.

items.main: Extends farm program authorities through crop year 2031, including ARC and PLC commodity support, Dairy Margin Coverage, and crop insurance enhancements.
items.detail: ARC and PLC payment limits increased to $155,000 per person (from $125,000), adjusted for inflation annually. The ARC program coverage guarantee increases from 86% to 90% of benchmark revenue; maximum payment amount increases from 10% to 12.5%. Crop insurance premium subsidies increase 3–5% depending on coverage level. The Supplemental Coverage Option (SCO) premium subsidy increases from 65% to 80%.

sections.label: Title II — Armed Services

items.main: Provides approximately $160 billion in FY2025 supplemental defense funding across shipbuilding, missile systems, space, nuclear forces, aircraft, and personnel.
items.detail: $29.2 billion for naval shipbuilding; $24.4 billion for missile defense and space-based sensors; $25.4 billion for hypersonic and other missiles; $16 billion for unmanned aerial systems and AI integration; $14.7 billion for nuclear forces including B-21 bomber expansion; $8.6 billion for aircraft modernization and prevention of F-22 retirement; $12.7 billion for Indo-Pacific military exercises and satellites; $7.5 billion for military quality of life including basic housing allowance and child care.

sections.label: Title VII — Individual and Business Tax Reforms

items.main: Permanently extends the individual income tax rates, standard deduction, and most deduction and credit provisions of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
items.detail: Standard deduction set at $15,750 for single filers and $31,500 for joint filers (inflation-adjusted). Estate tax exemption increased to $15 million. Child tax credit increased to $2,200 and indexed to inflation. SALT deduction cap raised to $40,000 through 2029, then reverts to $10,000. Qualified Business Income deduction made permanent with expanded phase-in range. Alternative minimum tax exemptions permanently raised.

items.main: Creates new above-the-line deductions for tip income (up to $25,000), overtime compensation (up to $12,500), and passenger vehicle loan interest (up to $10,000), all available for tax years 2025–2028.
items.detail: All three deductions phase out for individuals with modified AGI above $150,000 ($300,000 for joint filers) and require work-eligible Social Security numbers. A new "Trump account" IRA for individuals under 18 allows up to $5,000 annually; the federal government deposits a one-time $1,000 into accounts for children born in 2025–2028.

items.main: Extends 100% bonus depreciation permanently, allows immediate expensing of domestic R&D, and increases the Section 179 deduction limit to $2.5 million.
items.detail: Section 179 phase-out begins at $4 million in asset purchases. BEAT (base erosion minimum tax) rate reduced to 10.5% from 12.5% for tax years after 2025. GILTI and FDII renamed Net CFC Tested Income and Foreign-Derived Deduction Eligible Income, with the foreign tax credit haircut reduced from 20% to 10%.

items.main: Terminates most IRA clean energy tax credits for consumers and businesses, including EV credits, home efficiency credits, and wind and solar electricity credits.
items.detail: New and used EV credits terminated for vehicles purchased on or after October 1, 2025. Home energy efficiency and residential clean energy credits terminated effective 2026. Wind and solar clean electricity production and investment credits terminated for new projects placed in service after December 31, 2027. Clean hydrogen production credit terminated for construction beginning after 2027.

sections.label: Title VII — Medicaid and Medicare

items.main: Requires Medicaid expansion enrollees to complete 80 hours per month of work, community service, or education beginning in FY2027; states must redetermine expansion enrollees' eligibility every six months.
items.detail: Exemptions apply to individuals with serious medical conditions or dependent children aged 13 or younger. States may not waive the requirement, though the CMS may grant a state an implementation delay through December 31, 2028. Cost-sharing of up to $35 per service required for expansion enrollees with income above the poverty line beginning FY2029. Federal Medicaid payment suspended for one year for essential community providers with more than $800,000 in Medicaid revenue that furnish abortions outside of rape, incest, or life-threatening circumstances.

items.main: Reduces the maximum provider tax states may impose to fund Medicaid matching funds, phasing down to 3.5% by FY2032 from the current 6%.
items.detail: States that have not expanded Medicaid are precluded from increasing their provider tax rate. New provider taxes may not be created by states without an existing one. Medicaid and Medicare eligibility restricted to U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, and specified immigrant categories — excluding DACA recipients, TPS holders, asylees, and refugees beginning in FY2027 (Medicaid) and within 18 months of enactment (Medicare).

items.main: $10 billion per fiscal year for FY2026–FY2030 for a Rural Health Transformation Program providing states with funds to improve rural health access.
items.detail: 50% of funds distributed equally among approved states; remaining 50% based on proportion of rural health facilities. States must submit rural health transformation plans; no matching funds required. $200 million for FY2025 for CMS implementation.

sections.label: Title IX — Border Security and Homeland Security

items.main: Appropriates more than $109 billion through FY2029 for border barriers, CBP personnel, ICE detention, CBP surveillance equipment, and state border reimbursements.
items.detail: $46 billion to CBP for physical barriers, access roads, and detection technology; $45 billion to ICE for detention facility expansion; $12 billion for CBP personnel, bonuses, and fleet; $6 billion for CBP inspection and surveillance equipment; $10 billion to reimburse states and localities for border security actions taken on or after January 20, 2021.

items.main: $300 million to FEMA to reimburse state and local law enforcement for costs of protecting a presidential residence; $625 million for 2026 FIFA World Cup security and $1 billion for 2028 Olympics security.
items.detail: FEMA State Homeland Security Grant Program also receives $500 million for drone detection technology and $450 million for Operation Stonegarden border coordination through FY2029. The Federal Employees Health Benefits program receives $66 million for a mandatory eligibility audit to verify family members.

sections.label: Title X — Immigration, Judiciary, and Radiation Compensation

items.main: Establishes new or increased fees across the immigration system: $100 for asylum applications, $1,000 for parolees, $550 for asylee employment authorization, and $5,000 for individuals apprehended between ports of entry or ordered removed in absentia.
items.detail: $29 billion to ICE for hiring, removal operations, and detention; $3 billion to DOJ for immigration courts and drug trafficking prosecution; $3.5 billion to reimburse states for incarcerating non-citizen criminals; $5 billion for the Bureau of Prisons; $1 billion for the Secret Service. $100 fee per calendar year that an asylum application remains pending.

items.main: Reestablishes and expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation program through 2028, increasing compensation amounts and expanding geographic coverage to include additional areas of Idaho, New Mexico, Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, and Kentucky.
items.detail: Extends the statute of limitations for filing claims through 2027. Expands eligible groups to include additional uranium miners and individuals near Manhattan Project waste sites who developed certain cancers.

sections.label: Title V — Energy and Natural Resources

items.main: Reduces oil and gas royalty rates on federal lands, reinstates noncompetitive leasing, and mandates at least 4 ANWR lease sales and 5 NPR-A lease sales within 10 years.
items.detail: Offshore royalty rates also reduced; Gulf state revenue-sharing cap raised from $500 million to $650 million per year for FY2025–FY2034. Methane royalties on vented or flared gas from federal lands eliminated. $389 million for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; Biden-era mandatory drawdown repealed. Forest Service must sell 250 million board feet of additional timber per year through FY2034.

sections.label: Title VIII — Student Loans and Education

items.main: Eliminates Grad PLUS loans for new borrowers on or after July 1, 2026, and caps federal student borrowing at $100,000 aggregate for graduate students and $257,500 lifetime across all federal loan types.
items.detail: Parent PLUS loans capped at $20,000 annually and $65,000 lifetime per dependent undergraduate. All current income-based repayment plans (SAVE, PAYE, ICR) terminated for new loans; borrowers limited to a standard repayment plan or the new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP). Economic hardship and unemployment deferments eliminated for loans originated on or after July 1, 2027.

items.main: $10.5 billion in additional Pell Grant funding for FY2026; new Workforce Pell Grants created for programs of 150–600 clock hours in workforce training.
items.detail: Low-earning outcome programs — programs where graduates earn less than high school diploma holders — lose eligibility for federal funds beginning July 1, 2026. Institutions must notify enrolled students when a program loses eligibility. Borrower defense to repayment and closed school discharge regulations delayed until July 1, 2035.

sections.label: Title IV — Commerce, Transportation, and Infrastructure

items.main: $24.5 billion to the Coast Guard through FY2029 for new vessels, aircraft, and shore facilities; $12.52 billion to the FAA for facilities modernization including $4.75 billion for telecom infrastructure and $3 billion for radar replacement.
items.detail: FCC spectrum auction authority reauthorized through September 30, 2034; FCC must auction at least 300 MHz including 100 MHz in the Upper C-Band within two years; NTIA must identify 500 MHz of additional federal spectrum for reallocation within four years. CAFE standard civil penalty set to $0, eliminating enforcement.

items.main: $9.995 billion to NASA for Moon and Mars missions, ISS deorbit preparation, and Artemis IV and V spacecraft procurement; $9.995 billion includes a Mars telecommunications orbiter.
items.detail: NASA must identify a previously-flown crewed spacecraft to be relocated and placed on public display near a NASA field center within 18 months. Brand USA tourism promotion funding reduced from $100 million to $20 million per year through FY2027.

underreported.summary: Sets the civil penalty for a manufacturer's violation of CAFE fuel economy standards to $0, removing NHTSA's ability to enforce those standards through monetary penalties.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is titled and described as modifying the civil penalty amount, but the operative effect is to eliminate meaningful enforcement of federal fuel economy standards for automakers — a substantive change to federal vehicle emissions policy that is not referenced in the bill's title or stated purpose.

underreported.summary: Eliminates the $200 federal excise tax on the transfer of National Firearms Act items other than machine guns and destructive devices, effectively removing the tax on silencers, short-barreled rifles, and short-barreled shotguns.
underreported.why_unreported: The section appears in a tax chapter primarily focused on deductions and credits for families and businesses. The NFA excise tax removal is a standalone firearms regulatory change unrelated to the chapter's stated subject matter and is not mentioned in the bill's title.

underreported.summary: Prohibits federal Medicaid payment for one year to any nonprofit health care provider with more than $800,000 in annual Medicaid payments if the provider primarily furnishes family planning services and provides abortions outside of rape, incest, or life-threatening circumstances.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision is structured as a Medicaid payment restriction on a category of providers meeting specific criteria, but its operative effect — cutting off federal Medicaid funding to qualifying Planned Parenthood affiliates — is not stated in the section title or described in the bill's stated purposes.

underreported.summary: Eliminates the $800 de minimis customs exemption effective July 1, 2027, ending duty-free treatment for small-value imports that currently allows platforms like Shein and Temu to ship directly to U.S. consumers without tariffs.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision appears in a chapter captioned as enhancing deduction guardrails. It eliminates a longstanding customs exemption that has shaped the structure of direct-to-consumer international e-commerce, with broad implications for import pricing and retail competition not discussed in the bill's tax-focused framing.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Babin
featured_quotes.text: I rise today in very strong support of H.R. 1, President Trump's one big, beautiful bill. Here we are, despite months of our Democratic colleagues' best efforts to delay, fearmonger, and mislead the public about this bill, and we are ready to deliver for the American people. Here is the thing about fear-mongering. You can only say ``the sky is falling'' so many times before folks start waking up and seeing for themselves exactly what is going on. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act secures our border.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Brown
featured_quotes.text: For the first time in history, this bill would force States to pay for part of SNAP benefits, and it would require States to increase their share of administrative costs. This is an unfunded mandate, plain and simple. Let's be clear. The costs are staggering, the consequences are devastating, and the cruelty is deeply disturbing. This policy punishes those who can least afford it: seniors on a fixed income, veterans, and families already forced to choose between gas and groceries. States will be stuck in a corner.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Langworthy
featured_quotes.text: The stakes for the American people could not be higher. We are rapidly approaching a fiscal cliff. If we do nothing, the Trump tax cuts, the most progrowth tax reforms in generations, will expire. That means higher taxes on nearly every American. That means a gutted child tax credit. That means small businesses will lose the tools they need to survive and to thrive. That means less take-home pay for working families that have already been crushed by the Biden-era inflation. This isn't some hypothetical scenario.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, Republicans are openly bragging about how the bill kicks children and the elderly off Medicaid, nutritional assistance, and more, all to pay for another tax break for wealthy Republican donors. My Republican colleagues are not talking about the trillions and trillions of dollars their political giveaway is going to cost. In fact, Mr. Speaker, Vice President Vance has said historic levels of Homeland Security funding in the bill sweetens the deal for the devil.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Alford
featured_quotes.text: Today, Mr. Speaker, we face a watershed moment for the American people. This Republican majority was given a clear mandate by the American people, which is the America First agenda. This bill is our opportunity to deliver on that agenda. H.R. 1 stops the largest tax increase in U.S. history, while providing the largest tax cut for working-and middle-class families ever, with no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, and tax breaks for seniors.

gaps: The bill increases the statutory debt limit by $5 trillion but includes no spending cap, enforcement trigger, or fiscal review mechanism tied to the increase.

Medicaid work requirements are established for the expansion population but the bill specifies no federal remedy or enrollment fallback for individuals who lose coverage due to reporting failures unrelated to actual eligibility.

bills.title: Tribal Trust Land Homeownership Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to require the Bureau of Indian Affairs to process and complete all mortgage packages associated with residential and business mortgages on Indian land by certain deadlines, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) must now process mortgage applications on Indian trust land within strict deadlines — completing preliminary reviews within 10 days, and approving or disapproving leasehold mortgages within 20 days and land mortgages within 30 days. The law also creates a new Realty Ombudsman within the BIA to monitor compliance, serve as a liaison to federal mortgage agencies, and resolve complaints from tribes, tribal members, and lenders.
bills.brief: Sets mandatory processing deadlines for BIA mortgage packages on Indian trust land and creates a Realty Ombudsman to enforce compliance.

top_lines.headline: BIA Processing Deadlines
subs: Preliminary review of mortgage package within 10 calendar days of receipt
Leasehold mortgages approved or disapproved within 20 days; land mortgages and right-of-way documents within 30 days
First certified title status report completed within 14 days of request; subsequent reports within 10 days of approval

top_lines.headline: Delay Notification and System Access
subs: BIA must immediately notify affected parties upon missing any processing deadline
Must respond to all status inquiries within 2 calendar days
Relevant federal agencies and Indian Tribes receive read-only TAAMS portal access effective on enactment

top_lines.headline: Oversight and Reporting
subs: New Realty Ombudsman — a BIA official who monitors deadline compliance and resolves complaints from tribes and lenders — established within BIA Division of Real Estate Services
BIA Director must submit annual compliance report to Congress by March 1 each year
GAO must report on cost and feasibility of digitizing tribal mortgage records within 1 year

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on May 4, 2026 as Public Law 119-88. The bill passed both chambers with bipartisan support — it had 3 Senate cosponsors, a companion House bill (H.R. 2130) with a House Natural Resources Committee report, and cleared both the Senate Indian Affairs Committee and the House Natural Resources Committee before floor passage.

sections.label: Section 3 — Mortgage Review and Processing

items.main: BIA must complete preliminary review of any mortgage package within 10 calendar days of receipt, then approve or disapprove leasehold mortgages within 20 days and land mortgages or right-of-way documents within 30 days.
items.detail: Missing documents must be flagged to the lender within 2 calendar days of the preliminary review. Approval or disapproval decisions must be in writing; denials must state the basis. The 20-day leasehold approval deadline does not apply when the applicant is an Indian tribe approved for self-governance leasing under 25 U.S.C. § 415(h).

items.main: First certified title status reports must be completed within 14 calendar days of request; subsequent reports within 10 calendar days of mortgage approval — delivered directly to lenders, applicable bureau field offices, and relevant federal guarantor agencies.
items.detail: Notice of completion is provided electronically via secure encryption software and by U.S. mail; lenders may opt out of electronic delivery. If BIA misses any processing deadline, it must immediately notify all affected parties and respond to all subsequent status inquiries within 2 calendar days.

sections.label: Section 4 — Realty Ombudsman

items.main: The BIA Director must establish a Realty Ombudsman within the Division of Real Estate Services, reporting directly to the Secretary of the Interior.
items.detail: The Ombudsman monitors deadline compliance, ensures bureau offices comply with notification requirements, serves as a liaison to USDA, HUD, and VA on mortgage matters, and receives and resolves inquiries and complaints from Indian Tribes, tribal members, and lenders. The Comptroller General must submit to Congress a report on the cost and feasibility of digitizing tribal mortgage records within 1 year of enactment.

underreported.summary: The 20-day approval deadline for leasehold mortgages does not apply when the applicant is an Indian tribe approved for self-governance leasing under 25 U.S.C. § 415(h). Individual tribal members applying for mortgages on the same land remain subject to the full deadline regime.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around processing deadlines that apply uniformly to Indian land mortgages, but the operative exemption carves out tribal self-governance leasing activity from the 20-day approval requirement without any discussion in the bill title or stated purpose.

gaps: The bill requires annual reporting on deadline compliance by bureau office but specifies no penalties or corrective measures for offices that chronically miss the processing deadlines.
The bill title and purpose focus on homeownership, but the processing deadline framework applies equally to business leasehold mortgages and commercial right-of-way documents.
Read-only TAAMS portal access is granted to relevant federal agencies and Indian Tribes as institutional entities, but not to individual tribal members who are the direct mortgage applicants.

bills.title: Cashless Bail Reporting Act
bills.official_title: To direct the Attorney General to make publicly available a list of each State and unit of local government that permits cashless bail, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: The Attorney General must publish a list of every state and local government that allows defendants charged with crimes to be released before trial without posting cash — either on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond. The list must go up within 30 days of enactment and be updated every quarter.
bills.brief: Directs the Attorney General to publish and quarterly-update a public list of jurisdictions that permit pretrial release on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond.

top_lines.headline: Attorney General Publication Requirement
subs: Published list must identify every state and local government permitting personal recognizance or unsecured bond release
Initial publication required within 30 days of enactment; updated on a quarterly basis

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 308-116 — a margin indicating substantial Democratic crossover support, with roughly 80+ Democrats voting yes alongside the Republican majority. This bipartisan House coalition improves Senate prospects, but 60 Senate votes are still required to clear a filibuster. Cashless bail policy divides Senate Democrats, and no companion Senate bill has been identified. The crossover strength in the House is encouraging but not determinative.

sections.label: Section 2 — Publication of Cashless Bail Jurisdictions

items.main: The Attorney General must make publicly available a list of each state and unit of local government that permits pretrial release on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond within 30 days of enactment, updated quarterly.
items.detail: The publication requirement applies to any person charged with any offense — the bill text includes no limitation by offense type, severity, or category. No format, publication platform, or enforcement mechanism for failure to update is specified in the bill text.

underreported.summary: The list must cover jurisdictions that permit cashless bail for a person charged with any offense. The bill text contains no limitation to violent or serious crimes.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title and description reference cashless bail broadly, but the operative text applies the reporting requirement to releases for any charged offense with no category restriction — the bill covers misdemeanors and nonviolent charges as fully as violent ones.

gaps: The bill requires quarterly publication of the list but specifies no format, accessibility standard, or enforcement mechanism for failure to publish or update.

The bill covers release on personal recognizance and unsecured appearance bonds but does not address other low- or no-cash release mechanisms — property bonds, electronic monitoring conditions, or supervised release programs — that are not captured by the reporting requirement.

added: Requirement for Attorney General to publicly list all states and local governments permitting pretrial release on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond, published within 30 days and updated quarterly

bills.title: Monitor Accountability Act
bills.official_title: To provide for conditions on the appointment of monitors by courts, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Federal courts must follow new rules when appointing monitors to oversee state and local governments under consent decrees — including fee caps, a 5-year term limit, a one-monitorship-at-a-time restriction, and mandatory public notice before appointment. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts must issue rules within 90 days, and active monitorships already running 6 or more years must get a new monitor within 180 days and be transferred to a new judge within 1 year.
bills.brief: Sets term limits, fee caps, and public accountability rules for court-appointed monitors overseeing state and local governments under consent decrees.

top_lines.headline: Monitor Term and Appointment Limits
subs: 5-year term limit per court order; no reappointment under the same order after term expires
Monitor may not hold more than one monitorship at a time
Successor monitor may not be employed by the same firm as the prior monitor

top_lines.headline: Fee Caps and Public Accountability
subs: Fees capped at rates set by the Administrative Office of U.S. Courts; pro bono and reduced-rate services explicitly authorized
Annual public accounting of services, fees, and any pro bono work required from each monitor
Court must provide public notice and comment opportunity before appointing any monitor

top_lines.headline: Case Transfer and Retroactivity
subs: Case transferred to a new judge in the same district 6 years after the court order
Existing monitorships of 6+ years: new monitor appointed within 180 days of enactment, case transferred within 1 year

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 219-204 with only 5 crossover votes — a near party-line result indicating minimal Democratic support. Sponsor Rep. Biggs (R-AZ) had only 2 cosponsors. Consent decree reform is sharply partisan: term limits and fee caps would disrupt ongoing civil rights oversight of police departments, and Democratic senators are expected to oppose unanimously. The Senate 60-vote threshold is not within reach under current conditions.

sections.label: Section 2 — Conditions on Monitor Appointments

items.main: The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts must establish rules within 90 days imposing fee caps, a single-monitorship-at-a-time limit, a 5-year term limit with no reappointment under the same court order, and a prohibition on successive monitors sharing employers.
items.detail: Conditions apply to any person appointed by a district court to monitor the conduct of a state or unit of local government. Fee rules must explicitly authorize pro bono and reduced-rate services. Courts must provide public notice and an opportunity for comment before any monitor appointment.

items.main: Cases are transferred to a new judge in the same district 6 years after the court order imposing the monitorship; monitors must submit annual public accountings of services, fees, and pro bono work to the court.
items.detail: For monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years on the date of enactment, a new monitor must be appointed within 180 days and the case transferred within 1 year. The transfer trigger is purely time-based with no assessment of compliance status required.

underreported.summary: The retroactivity clause requires all monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years to appoint a new monitor within 180 days and transfer the case to a new judge within 1 year, regardless of whether the monitored entity is making progress toward compliance.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around appointment conditions for future monitorships, but Section 2(d) immediately disrupts currently active consent decree oversight arrangements — including ongoing policing reform monitorships — without any compliance-status prerequisite.

underreported.summary: Cases transfer to a new judge automatically at exactly 6 years after the court order on a time-based trigger with no assessment of case status, compliance progress, or complexity.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill purpose covers appointment conditions, but the judge-transfer provision operates as a mandatory procedural reset on a fixed schedule independent of whether the monitorship is progressing toward its stated goals.

gaps: The bill sets a 5-year term limit for monitors but specifies no continuity procedure if no compliant replacement monitor can be identified or appointed before the prior monitor's term expires.

The bill scope covers monitors appointed to oversee state and local governments but does not address monitors appointed in deferred prosecution agreements with private entities or federal contractors, which operate under the same district court rules.

Prohibition on successive monitors under the same court order sharing the same employer
Public notice and comment requirement before any monitor appointment

Mandatory case transfer to a new judge 6 years after the court order

bills.title: Keeping Violent Offenders Off Our Streets Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend title 18, United States Code, to prohibit fraud in connection with posting bail.
bills.summary: This bill adds the posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and federal immigration bail bonds to the federal definition of the "business of insurance" — making organizations that post bail, including charitable bail funds, subject to federal insurance fraud criminal statutes and state insurance licensing requirements.
bills.brief: Expands the federal definition of "business of insurance" to include bail-posting activity, subjecting charitable bail funds and bail bond companies to federal insurance fraud law.

top_lines.headline: Bail Redefined as Insurance Activity
subs: Adds posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and federal immigration bail bonds to the federal definition of "business of insurance"
Subjects bail-posting entities — including charitable bail organizations — to federal criminal fraud and embezzlement provisions that apply to insurance companies

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 243-179 with 33 crossover votes — some bipartisan support, but the mechanism (reclassifying bail-posting entities as insurance companies) remains a partisan flash point. In the Senate, 60 votes are needed to clear a filibuster. Most Democratic senators are expected to oppose a provision that would subject charitable bail funds to federal criminal liability, and no Senate companion bill has been identified.

sections.label: Section 2 — Fraud in Connection with Posting Bail

items.main: Amends 18 U.S.C. 1033(f)(1)(A) to add "the posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and Federal immigration bail bonds" to the existing definition of the business of insurance.
items.detail: Under 18 U.S.C. 1033, persons engaged in the business of insurance are subject to federal criminal penalties for embezzlement, false statements, and related fraud. After this amendment, entities that post bail — including charitable bail organizations — are subject to those criminal provisions and, by extension, to state insurance licensing requirements and regulation by state insurance commissioners.

underreported.summary: The amendment to 18 U.S.C. 1033(f)(1)(A) extends the federal insurance fraud criminal statute to bail-posting entities. Officers, directors, and employees of organizations that post bail could face federal criminal liability for embezzlement or false statements under 1033 — not limited to bail posted for violent offenders.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title references violent offenders, but the operative amendment applies to all bail posting without any offense-type limitation. The mechanism operates through the insurance fraud statute, making the primary legal effect a reclassification that triggers criminal exposure rather than a direct restriction on bail practices.

gaps: The bill amends the "business of insurance" definition but specifies no threshold — in frequency, dollar amount, or organizational structure — at which a bail-posting entity crosses into engaging in the "business" of insurance versus making an occasional bail payment.

The amendment covers criminal bail bonds and federal immigration bail bonds but does not address civil immigration bonds maintained under a separate regulatory regime, which are not referenced in the amendment text.

modified: 18 U.S.C. 1033(f)(1)(A) — definition of "business of insurance" expanded to include the posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and federal immigration bail bonds

bills.title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
bills.summary: For decades, families of Holocaust victims have tried to recover artwork stolen by Nazi Germany, only to have American courts dismiss their cases on procedural grounds — time delays, deference to foreign governments, or doctrines unrelated to who actually owned the art. This law permanently removes those barriers. It prohibits courts from dismissing Holocaust art claims based on the passage of time or other procedural defenses, strips foreign governments of a key immunity argument regardless of the victim's nationality, removes the December 31, 2026 filing deadline entirely, and applies all of those changes retroactively to cases currently in court.
bills.brief: Permanently bars courts from dismissing Nazi-looted art claims on procedural grounds, overriding multiple appellate and Supreme Court rulings that had blocked recovery.

top_lines.headline: Procedural Defenses Eliminated
subs: Laches, adverse possession, international comity, forum non conveniens, and act of state doctrine may no longer be used to dismiss Holocaust art claims
Applies retroactively to cases currently pending, including those on appeal

top_lines.headline: Foreign Sovereign Immunity Overridden
subs: Claims against foreign governments proceed regardless of victim nationality — overrides the 2021 Supreme Court ruling in Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp
Nationwide service of process added, allowing courts to reach defendants in any U.S. district

top_lines.headline: Filing Deadline Removed
subs: December 31, 2026 filing deadline eliminated — claims may be filed at any time
Six-year discovery period from the date the claimant learns of the artwork's location still applies

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 13, 2026 as Public Law 119-82.

sections.label: Section 2 — Prohibited Defenses

items.main: Adds new Section 5(f) to the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016, barring all time-based defenses and all non-merits discretionary bases for dismissal against otherwise timely Holocaust art claims.
items.detail: Prohibited time-based defenses include laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription, and usucapion. Prohibited non-merits defenses include the act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, and prudential exhaustion. The bill adds findings naming specific court decisions that frustrated the original Act's intent, including Zuckerman v. Metropolitan Museum of Art (2d Cir. 2019), Cassirer v. Thyssen-Bornemisza Foundation (9th Cir. 2024), and Von Saher v. Norton Simon Museum of Art (9th Cir. 2018).

sections.label: Section 2 — Foreign State Jurisdiction and Retroactive Application

items.main: New Section 5(b) deems Holocaust art claims to constitute actions involving violations of international law for purposes of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(3)), regardless of the nationality or citizenship of the alleged victim.
items.detail: This directly overrides Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, 592 U.S. 169 (2021), in which the Supreme Court held that the "domestic takings" rule barred FSIA jurisdiction over property seized from a country's own nationals. Nationwide service of process is added for all civil actions under the Act. All amendments apply to claims pending on the date of enactment — including cases pending on appeal or within the appeal filing window — and to cases filed after enactment.

items.main: Removes the December 31, 2026 deadline for filing claims and replaces it with a perpetual filing window subject to a six-year discovery period.
items.detail: Under prior law, all claims had to be filed by December 31, 2026 regardless of when the claimant discovered the property's location. This deadline is eliminated. Claims must still be filed within six years of the claimant's discovery of the property in question.

underreported.summary: The law applies to any civil claim pending in any court on the date of enactment, including claims pending on appeal and claims for which the time to file an appeal has not yet expired.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is the permanent removal of procedural barriers to future claims. The retroactive reach to cases already dismissed and currently on appeal means courts that previously dismissed Holocaust art claims on laches or international comity grounds could have those dismissals challenged or reversed under the new law, affecting outcomes in litigation already underway.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Raskin
featured_quotes.text: This bill, which has already passed the Senate by unanimous consent, amends the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016 in a number of key ways to ensure that Holocaust survivors and their heirs have a fair opportunity in court to recover all of the artwork that was stolen by the Nazi regime or what is left of it. In doing so, this bill will provide these victims the chance to obtain some small measure of justice for the horrors and the injustices and indignities their families have endured.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lee
featured_quotes.text: it is just for Holocaust survivors and their heirs to continue to have their claims relating to art stolen from them  by the Nazis heard in court. These claims should be decided on the merits, not dismissed due to technical defenses. The Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025 will ensure just that.

gaps: The law bars procedural defenses but does not address the evidentiary standard for establishing provenance or Nazi-era confiscation in the underlying merits of a claim.

The law covers artwork lost "because, or as a result, of Nazi persecution" but does not address property transferred through forced sales under economic duress rather than outright confiscation, a category that has faced definitional challenges in prior litigation.

added: Section 5(b) of the HEAR Act — foreign sovereign immunity exception: Holocaust art claims deemed violations of international law under 28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(3) regardless of victim nationality

Section 5(f) — prohibition on all time-based defenses (laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription, usucapion) and non-merits discretionary defenses (act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, prudential exhaustion)
Section 5(g) — nationwide service of process for Holocaust art civil actions
Section 6 — severability provision
modified: HEAR Act of 2016 findings — expanded to name specific court decisions that frustrated the Act's intent and to state that non-merits defenses must be precluded
HEAR Act Section 3(2) — definition of covered defenses expanded to include "other non-merits defenses" alongside statutes of limitation
removed: December 31, 2026 filing deadline for Holocaust art recovery claims

bills.title: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act
bills.official_title: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act
bills.summary: The SBIR and STTR programs are the federal government's primary mechanism for funding early-stage technology research at small businesses — agencies with large R&D budgets must set aside a percentage for competitive grants to startups, covering everything from initial feasibility through full development and commercialization. This law extends those programs through fiscal year 2031 and adds a significant national security layer: agencies must now screen all applicants against eight federal watchlists for foreign adversary connections, can deny grants based on classified intelligence, and must notify rejected applicants of the basis for denial when doing so won't compromise national security.
bills.brief: Extends SBIR and STTR small-business research grants through FY2031 and adds mandatory screening against eight federal watchlists for foreign adversary ties.

top_lines.headline: Extended Through FY2031
subs: SBIR and STTR programs reauthorized through fiscal year 2031
New strategic breakthrough allocations added — Phase II awards for critical technology areas requiring matching funds

top_lines.headline: Eight-Watchlist Security Screen
subs: Applicants checked against UFLPA, OFAC Chinese Military-Industrial Complex, Section 889, Chinese Military Companies, Military End User, Entity, FCC Equipment, and CBP Withhold Release Orders lists
Classified security risks are also a basis for denial; rejected applicants must be notified of the basis unless doing so would compromise national security

top_lines.headline: Caps and Commercialization
subs: Maximum number of proposals per small business per fiscal year established for Phase I and Phase II
Expanded Phase III commercialization training required for agency contracting officers

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 13, 2026 as Public Law 119-83.

sections.label: Section 2 — Security Risk Evaluation

items.main: Requires federal agencies administering SBIR and STTR programs to evaluate whether applicants present security risks, including through coordination with the intelligence community, law enforcement, and other counterintelligence capabilities.
items.detail: Agencies must deny applications from small businesses with a security risk connecting them to entities or individuals on any of eight federal watchlists: the UFLPA Entity List (DHS), the OFAC Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List (Treasury), the Section 889 Prohibition List (DoD), the Chinese Military Companies List (DoD), the Military End User List (Commerce), the Entity List (Commerce), the FCC Equipment and Services List, or the CBP Withhold Release Orders and Findings List. Classified security risks and agency-determined security risks are also grounds for denial. Upon denying an application on security grounds, the agency must notify the small business of the determination and its basis, to the extent doing so does not compromise national security. Denial on security grounds does not bar the business from applying in a subsequent award cycle.

sections.label: Sections 3–End — Extension, Caps, and Strategic Allocations

items.main: Reauthorizes SBIR and STTR programs through fiscal year 2031 and caps the number of Phase I and Phase II proposals any single small business may submit per fiscal year.
items.detail: The proposal cap prevents a single small business from monopolizing agency review bandwidth. The bill also expands training requirements for agencies' contracting officers regarding Phase III commercialization awards, which involve agencies purchasing or licensing SBIR/STTR-developed technologies without a separate competitive bid requirement.

items.main: Establishes strategic breakthrough allocations — additional Phase II SBIR and STTR awards for small businesses in critical technology areas that demonstrate effective technology and secure matching funds.
items.detail: The matching fund requirement for strategic breakthrough allocations is intended to attract private co-investment alongside the federal award. Critical technology areas are not defined in the bill; determination is left to the administering agencies.

underreported.summary: Agencies may deny SBIR/STTR applications based on a security risk whose primary source is classified, without being required to disclose the basis for denial.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's security screening is presented as a watchlist-based transparency mechanism. The classified-source denial pathway allows rejection without any meaningful notification — the agency's only obligation is to tell the applicant a determination was made, not why, leaving the small business with no basis to challenge or cure the disqualification.

gaps: The bill requires agencies to notify denied applicants of the basis for security-related rejections but provides no appeal or reconsideration process for small businesses that dispute a watchlist-based determination.

Strategic breakthrough allocations target "critical technology areas" but the bill does not define or enumerate those areas, leaving the scope of the new allocation category entirely to agency discretion.

added: Requirement for SBIR and STTR agencies to evaluate security risks of applicants through watchlist screening, intelligence community coordination, and classified risk assessment
Eight-watchlist disqualification framework for SBIR and STTR applicants with foreign adversary connections
Notification requirement for security-based denials, to the extent consistent with national security
Maximum proposal cap per small business per fiscal year for Phase I and Phase II solicitations
Strategic breakthrough allocations — additional Phase II awards for critical technology areas requiring matching private funds
modified: SBIR and STTR program authorization extended through fiscal year 2031
Phase III commercialization training requirements for agency contracting officers expanded

bills.title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
bills.official_title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
bills.summary: Federal tax law normally requires casualty losses to exceed 10% of your income before you can deduct them — but Congress has repeatedly carved out exceptions for federally declared disaster areas, letting affected taxpayers deduct unreimbursed losses above $500 per incident even without itemizing. This bill extends those disaster-specific deduction rules to cover disasters with incident periods beginning before January 1, 2027 (up from the prior cutoff of July 4, 2025), and extends the exclusion of wildfire relief payments from taxable income to fires declared a federal disaster before 2027.
bills.brief: Extends the federal tax deduction for disaster property losses and the wildfire relief payment exclusion to disasters occurring before January 1, 2027.

top_lines.headline: Disaster Loss Deductions
subs: Extended to disasters with incident periods beginning before January 1, 2027 — up from July 4, 2025
Deductible without itemizing; exempt from the alternative minimum tax

top_lines.headline: Wildfire Relief Payments
subs: Relief payments for fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and before 2027 excluded from gross income
Currently capped at fires declared before 2026 and payments received before 2026

bills.likelihoodReason: Disaster tax relief has consistent bipartisan support and 14 cosponsors. Extension bills of this type routinely pass the Senate, often attached to larger tax packages. The geographic scope — covering presidentially declared disasters nationwide — limits targeted opposition.

sections.label: Section 2 — Disaster Casualty Loss Deduction

items.main: Adds Section 165(h)(6) to the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, creating a special deduction category for qualified net disaster losses that bypasses the 10% adjusted gross income limitation.
items.detail: A qualified net disaster loss is the excess of qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses over personal casualty gains. A qualified disaster area covers any area with a presidential major disaster declaration under section 401 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act where the incident period begins after July 4, 2025, and before January 1, 2027. Disaster losses may be deducted as part of the standard deduction under new Section 63(c)(1)(C) and are exempt from the alternative minimum tax under Section 56(b)(1)(D).

sections.label: Section 3 — Wildfire Relief Payment Exclusion

items.main: Creates new Section 139M of the Internal Revenue Code, excluding qualified wildfire relief payments from gross income.
items.detail: The exclusion applies to payments for forest or range fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and before 2027, regardless of when such payments are received. Under prior law, the exclusion applied only to qualifying payments received after 2019 and before 2026.

underreported.summary: The bill explicitly exempts the disaster loss deduction from the alternative minimum tax by amending Section 56(b)(1)(D) of the Internal Revenue Code.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is extension of the disaster deduction window. The AMT exception means taxpayers who would otherwise owe AMT — typically higher earners — retain the full value of the deduction, a consequence not apparent from the disaster relief framing.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steube
featured_quotes.text: When hurricanes, wildfires, floods, tornadoes, and other disasters strike, American families are left to rebuild their homes, their businesses, their communities, and their lives. When these moments arise, the last thing they need is the Federal Government making their recovery harder by taxing relief payments or denying fair treatment for disaster losses, nor should the government be creating uncertainty in the tax code.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Panetta
featured_quotes.text: I support the Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act. I am a proud cosponsor, co-lead of this bill with Representatives Greg Steube and Mike Thompson, a bill that would build on the Federal Disaster Tax Relief Act which we passed last Congress, thanks to the leadership of Representative Steube, a bill that would ensure that those impacted by disasters nationwide have continued access to tax relief.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fong
featured_quotes.text: In California, we are all too familiar with the devastation caused by wildfires. After these disasters strike in our community, survivors shouldn't have to worry about burdensome Federal taxes as they work to recover and rebuild. Today, we have an opportunity to address that while honoring my friend the late Doug LaMalfa, who was a tireless champion of rural California and an advocate for those rebuilding after wildfires.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Tokuda
featured_quotes.text: I rise today, like so many of my colleagues on both sides of the aisle, to honor our friend Doug LaMalfa. He understood that the disaster after the disaster happens when families cannot recover and return to their hometowns because the funding and resources they receive just don't stretch far enough or, worse, are taxed and taken away from people who need absolutely every single dollar to be able to rebuild. On Saturday, I stood above Lahaina, and for a moment--the briefest of moments--in the darkness, the town almost looked normal.

gaps: The bill covers disasters with incident periods beginning before January 1, 2027, but does not address losses sustained within a qualified disaster area where the damage is discovered or claims are settled after January 1, 2027.

The wildfire relief exclusion applies only to fires paired with a federal disaster declaration and does not address relief payments from state programs for fires that did not receive a federal declaration.

Section 63(c)(1)(C) — disaster loss deduction available as part of the standard deduction
Section 139M — exclusion from gross income for qualified wildfire relief payments for fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and before 2027
modified: Section 56(b)(1)(D) of the Internal Revenue Code — disaster loss deduction exempted from the alternative minimum tax
Definition of qualified disaster area extended to incident periods beginning after July 4, 2025, and before January 1, 2027

bills.title: Clergy Act
bills.official_title: Clergy Act
bills.summary: Ordained ministers and Christian Science practitioners can apply to permanently opt out of Social Security and Medicare taxes on their ministerial earnings — but that exemption is currently irrevocable. This bill creates a one-time window for those who previously opted out to reverse that decision and re-enter the Social Security system, with coverage beginning for taxable years starting after December 31, 2027. Once revoked, they cannot opt out again.
bills.brief: Creates a one-time window for clergy who opted out of Social Security to reverse that decision and begin accruing retirement benefits.

top_lines.headline: One-Time Re-entry Window
subs: Clergy may revoke their Social Security exemption by filing through the deadline for their second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027
Coverage begins for taxable years starting after December 31, 2027 — cannot opt out again after revoking

top_lines.headline: IRS Outreach Required
subs: Commissioner of Internal Revenue must submit a plan to inform eligible clergy of their eligibility within 90 days of enactment

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has 21 cosponsors and bipartisan backing — sponsors include Fong (R-CA), Thompson (D-CA), and Kelly (R-PA). Providing clergy a window to undo a permanent decision is unlikely to draw opposition. The narrow scope and sympathetic affected population make Senate passage plausible, though floor scheduling is uncertain.

sections.label: Section 2 — Revocation of Social Security Exemption

items.main: Notwithstanding Section 1402(e)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code (which makes the Social Security exemption irrevocable), clergy whose exemption is in effect for the taxable year of enactment may revoke it by filing an application with the IRS.
items.detail: The application must be filed no later than the due date for the second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027. Revocation takes effect for the first or second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027, as specified by the applicant, and covers both chapter 2 of the IRC (self-employment tax) and title II of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 401 et seq.). If the application is filed retroactively for a year already in effect, the applicant must pay in full all self-employment taxes that would have been owed for that year. After revoking, the applicant may not again file for an exemption under Section 1402(e)(1).

sections.label: Section 3 — IRS Outreach Plan

items.main: The Commissioner of Internal Revenue, in consultation with the Commissioner of Social Security, must develop and submit a plan to inform eligible clergy of their revocation eligibility within 90 days of enactment.
items.detail: The plan must be submitted to the Ways and Means Committee of the House and the Finance Committee of the Senate. No minimum outreach activities, funding level, or success metrics are specified in the bill.

underreported.summary: If a clergy member files a revocation application after the due date for a taxable year and elects to have it take effect for that year, they must immediately pay all self-employment taxes that would have been owed for the entire year.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is a window to opt back in. The catch-up payment requirement means that choosing early retroactive coverage triggers a lump-sum tax obligation for the full year of retroactive coverage — a condition not apparent from the bill's title or the primary revocation provision.

gaps: The bill allows revocation effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027 but does not address Social Security credits for prior years during which the exemption was in effect — those years generate no credits regardless of revocation.
The 90-day outreach plan requirement specifies no minimum outreach activities, distribution channels, or funding, leaving the scope of IRS notification entirely to agency discretion.

added: One-time window for clergy and Christian Science practitioners to revoke their irrevocable Social Security exemption under Section 1402(e)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027
Requirement for the Commissioner of Internal Revenue to submit an outreach plan to inform eligible clergy within 90 days of enactment
