bills.title: Taxpayer Experience Improvement Act
bills.official_title: Taxpayer Experience Improvement Act
bills.summary: This bill requires the IRS to publish real-time data on its public website about phone wait times, call volumes, and processing backlogs for every public phone line it operates, and to make that data available through a public API so third-party apps can display it. It also requires the IRS to give taxpayers online or mobile access to their own tax returns, notices, and refund status including an estimated delivery date.
bills.brief: Requires the IRS to publish live phone wait times and backlog data, and give taxpayers digital access to their own returns and refund status.

top_lines.headline: Real-Time IRS Dashboard
subs: IRS must publish live caller counts, wait times, and callback availability per phone line on its public website
Public API required so any person or app can access the live call data

top_lines.headline: Digital Tax Record Access
subs: Taxpayers can view all returns, notices, and IRS letters via website or mobile app
IRS must provide estimated refund receipt date

top_lines.headline: Monthly Accountability Metrics
subs: IRS must publish monthly averages for call length, hold time, disconnection rate, and percent of callers who got help
Sense of Congress: callback offered within 5 minutes on any unanswered call by 2028

bills.likelihoodReason: Only 1 cosponsor despite bipartisan sponsorship (Schweikert R-AZ and Beyer D-VA). IRS modernization bills often pass the House but stall in the Senate amid disagreements over IRS funding and IT capacity. The real-time dashboard and public API requirements may face resistance from the Treasury Department over implementation feasibility.

sections.label: Section 2 — Public Wait Time Dashboard

items.main: Requires the IRS to publish in real time on its public website call volume, wait time, and callback availability for each applicable phone number extension.
items.detail: For each phone line, the IRS must display the number of callers connected to representatives, connected to automated systems, and waiting; the longest current wait time; and whether callback service is available. A public API must be provided for automated access to the data. The IRS must also detect and screen automated calls, and publish processing delay information weekly when significant backlogs occur.

items.main: Requires monthly summary statistics for each phone line, including caller satisfaction data.
items.detail: Monthly metrics must include average and median call lengths and hold times; the percent of calls disconnected or directed to automation; the number of callers transferred; and the number and percent of callers who indicated they received the help they were seeking. The last metric requires the IRS to actively collect caller satisfaction data before calls end.

sections.label: Sections 3–5 — Digital Access, Callbacks, and Online Accounts

items.main: Requires the IRS to make available to taxpayers — via website or mobile application — their tax returns, documents, all notices and letters sent by or to the IRS, refund status, and an estimated refund receipt date.
items.detail: The bill also expresses the sense of Congress that by 2028 the IRS should offer a callback to any caller not answered within five minutes, and requires expansion of online taxpayer account access.

underreported.summary: The monthly statistics requirement includes the number and percent of callers who indicated they received the answers or service they were seeking — a customer satisfaction data point embedded in a call-volume reporting requirement.
underreported.why_unreported: Collecting this metric requires the IRS to actively ask callers before they hang up whether their issue was resolved, effectively mandating a caller survey process. This is a new operational requirement distinct from passively logging call volume and wait times, not apparent from the bill's IRS dashboard framing.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Schweikert
featured_quotes.text: I ask the chairman whether it is tireless or annoying. It is one or the other. Look, I have an absolute fixation, and I have got to thank my Democratic colleague and a number of the team here for tolerating my fixation on the fact that one of the ways you work within the IRS budget to make things more efficient is the adoption of technology. Imagine a world--because it is the one we live in--where some of the number one calls we get to my district office are IRS questions: Where is my refund? Do I owe money?

gaps: The bill requires real-time call data but does not specify a minimum uptime requirement for the dashboard or what disclosures are required if the live data is unavailable.
The digital access requirement does not specify an implementation timeline for the mobile application option, nor minimum device or accessibility standards for the application.

added: Requirement for real-time IRS public dashboard with per-phone-line call volume, wait times, and callback availability, plus public API access
Monthly IRS reporting requirement including caller satisfaction metrics, disconnection rates, and hold times per phone extension
Requirement for IRS to provide taxpayers with online or mobile access to returns, notices, refund status, and estimated refund date
Requirement for IRS to use technology to detect and screen automated calls

bills.title: Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act
bills.official_title: Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act
bills.summary: When the IRS wants information about you from a third party like your employer or bank, current law requires it to notify you in advance — but not what specific information it's seeking. This bill requires the IRS to identify each specific item of information it intends to collect from the third party, and give you at least 45 days to provide it yourself, whenever the IRS hasn't already asked you for it and you could reasonably provide it. Two exceptions apply: the rule doesn't cover tax collection proceedings, and the Secretary can waive it when third-party contact is deemed necessary.
bills.brief: Requires the IRS to tell taxpayers exactly what information it plans to collect from third parties and give them 45 days to provide it first.

top_lines.headline: Specific Notice Required
subs: IRS must identify each item sought from a third party when the taxpayer hasn't been asked before and could provide it
Taxpayers get at least 45 days to respond — more if they request it with reasonable cause

top_lines.headline: Exceptions
subs: Specificity requirement waived for tax collection proceedings or when Secretary determines third-party contact is necessary regardless

bills.likelihoodReason: Only 1 cosponsor and a narrow taxpayer privacy focus. The IRS exemption allowing the Secretary to waive specificity requirements whenever deemed necessary limits the bill's practical effect, which may reduce the urgency Senate sponsors attach to it. IRS procedural reform bills without broad coalition backing rarely advance quickly in the Senate.

sections.label: Section 2 — Specificity of Third-Party Contact Notices

items.main: Amends Section 7602(c)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to require the IRS to identify each specific item of information it intends to seek from a third party when that information has not been previously requested from the taxpayer and could reasonably be provided by the taxpayer.
items.detail: The advance notice must provide the taxpayer with a period of not less than 45 days — or more if the taxpayer requests additional time and shows reasonable cause — to respond, including by providing the information themselves, before the IRS contacts the third party. The exception in Section 7602(c)(3)(B) provides that the specificity and waiting period requirements do not apply if the information is sought for collection of a tax liability, or if the Secretary determines the third-party information is necessary regardless of whether the taxpayer could provide it. Effective date: 12 months after enactment.

underreported.summary: The bill's specificity and 45-day notice requirements do not apply whenever the Secretary determines that the third-party information is necessary, without any standard for what constitutes necessity or any procedural check on that determination.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed as expanding taxpayer notification rights. The necessity exception allows the IRS to bypass both the itemized notice and the 45-day waiting period entirely based on the Secretary's own judgment, with no defined standard, independent review, or notification to the taxpayer that the exception has been invoked.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steube
featured_quotes.text: At its core, this commonsense legislation is a simple due process idea: Before the IRS goes to your bank, your employer, your vendor, or another third party for information about you, when you can reasonably provide that information yourself, you should be told what they are looking for and given a fair chance to respond. Under current law, taxpayers can receive a general third-party contact notice, but too often those notices aren't specific enough to let a person meaningfully respond.

gaps: The bill requires the IRS to give the taxpayer 45 days to respond but does not specify whether the IRS is barred from contacting the third party if the taxpayer provides the requested information within the window.

The bill does not address the taxpayer's right to receive notice that the Secretary has invoked the necessity exception, leaving taxpayers without information about why the standard procedure was not followed.

added: Section 7602(c)(1)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code — requirement for IRS to identify each specific item of information sought from a third party when not previously requested from the taxpayer
Section 7602(c)(1)(C) amendment — 45-day minimum response period before third-party contact, with extensions available on reasonable cause

bills.title: New Opportunities for Business Ownership and Self-Sufficiency Act
bills.official_title: New Opportunities for Business Ownership and Self-Sufficiency Act
bills.summary: Self-Employment Assistance programs let unemployed workers collect their unemployment benefits as a lump-sum allowance while they start a business, instead of conducting a traditional job search. This bill doubles the cap on program participation from 5% to 10% of unemployment recipients per state, removes the requirement that participants be on track to exhaust their benefits, adds a weekly self-certification requirement, and creates an alternative qualification pathway through a state-approved business plan rather than requiring formal entrepreneurial training.
bills.brief: Doubles state SEA program participation to 10%, drops the exhaustion-of-benefits eligibility requirement, and adds a business-plan qualification pathway.

top_lines.headline: Expanded Access
subs: Removes the requirement that participants be likely to exhaust unemployment benefits — opens programs to more applicants
Business plan + market feasibility study now qualifies as an alternative to formal entrepreneurial training

top_lines.headline: Larger Programs, Weekly Accountability
subs: State participation cap raised from 5% to 10% of unemployment benefit recipients
Participants must certify their self-employment activities on at least a weekly basis

bills.likelihoodReason: Bipartisan sponsorship (Carey R-OH and Landsman D-OH among others) and 6 cosponsors. Small business and entrepreneurship provisions attract broad support, but the 2-year implementation delay and required Labor Department rulemaking introduce uncertainty. Senate floor time for unemployment program reforms is limited.

sections.label: Section 2 — Modified SEA Program Requirements

items.main: Amends Section 3306(t) of the Internal Revenue Code to remove the requirement that SEA participants be identified as likely to exhaust regular unemployment compensation benefits, expanding the eligible population.
items.detail: Subparagraph (B) of Section 3306(t)(3), which required participants to be identified as likely to exhaust benefits, is stricken. Eligible self-employment activities may now qualify through either (i) the existing path of entrepreneurial training, business counseling, and technical assistance approved by the state, or (ii) a new path through a business plan and market feasibility study submitted by the individual and approved by the state or a designated agency. Participants must certify their activities at least weekly to a state-designated agency.

items.main: Raises the state SEA program participation cap from 5% to 10% of individuals receiving regular unemployment compensation.
items.detail: The change to Section 3306(t)(4) doubles the maximum share of unemployment benefit recipients a state may enroll in its SEA program. Changes take effect 2 years after enactment; states may amend their laws before then. The Secretary of Labor must adopt implementing regulations through public notice and comment, subject to OMB approval.

underreported.summary: The bill's changes do not take effect until 2 years after enactment, and states must amend their own laws within that window to be compliant.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's operative changes — expanded eligibility, the business-plan pathway, and the higher participation cap — are the headline. The 2-year gap before any of those changes can be used, combined with the requirement for state-level legislative action, means the bill's benefits may not materialize in states that fail to update their laws in time.

gaps: The bill doubles participation caps and expands eligibility but does not address the funding source for increased SEA allowances, which are paid from state unemployment trust funds that vary significantly in reserves across states.
The bill adds a weekly certification requirement but does not specify consequences for participants who miss certifications or the process for removing a non-compliant participant.

added: Business plan and market feasibility study as an alternative qualifying pathway for SEA program activities under Section 3306(t)(3)
Weekly self-certification requirement for SEA program participants
modified: Section 3306(t)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code — eliminated the requirement that participants be identified as likely to exhaust regular unemployment compensation benefits
Section 3306(t)(4) — state SEA program participation cap raised from 5% to 10% of unemployment benefit recipients
removed: Section 3306(t)(3)(B) — requirement that SEA participants be likely to exhaust unemployment benefits

bills.title: Supporting Early-childhood Educators' Deductions Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Supporting Early-childhood Educators' Deductions Act of 2025
bills.summary: K-12 teachers can deduct up to $300 per year in unreimbursed classroom expenses directly from their gross income without itemizing — but pre-K and early childhood educators are currently excluded. This bill extends that deduction to teachers and staff at schools providing early childhood education. It applies retroactively starting with tax year 2025.
bills.brief: Extends the $300 above-the-line educator expense deduction to early childhood and pre-K educators, retroactive to tax year 2025.

top_lines.headline: Expanded Educator Deduction
subs: Early childhood educators added to the up-to-$300 above-the-line deduction for unreimbursed classroom expenses
Retroactive to expenses incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024

top_lines.headline: Who Qualifies
subs: Teachers, instructors, counselors, principals, and aides in schools providing early childhood (pre-kindergarten) education
23 bipartisan cosponsors; eligibility criteria otherwise unchanged from existing K-12 provision

bills.likelihoodReason: Strong bipartisan support with 23 cosponsors. Expanding educator tax benefits is a consistently popular, low-controversy issue in both chambers. The retroactive application to tax year 2025 creates urgency for Senate passage. The narrow, targeted nature of the change limits points of opposition.

sections.label: Section 2 — Educator Expense Deduction for Early Childhood Educators

items.main: Amends Section 62 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to add early childhood educators to the above-the-line deduction for eligible educator expenses.
items.detail: Section 62(d)(1)(A) is amended to insert "early childhood educator" before "kindergarten through grade 12 teacher," and Section 62(d)(1)(B) is amended to include "early childhood education" and "pre-kindergarten" alongside elementary and secondary education. The heading of Section 62(a)(2)(D) is updated to reflect the expanded scope. The deduction limit — up to $300 in 2025, adjusted annually — and all other existing eligibility conditions are unchanged. Effective for expenses incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

underreported.summary: The bill inserts "early childhood educator" into the eligibility definition without providing a statutory definition of who qualifies as an early childhood educator or what constitutes a school providing early childhood education.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's purpose is to close the gap between K-12 and pre-K eligibility. The undefined terms leave it to the IRS to determine whether providers such as home daycares, private preschools, federally-funded Head Start centers, or school-district pre-K classrooms qualify — a scope determination with significant reach.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, in Pennsylvania, more than 68,000 early-childhood educators support our youngest learners every single day. The first 5 years of a child's life lay down the foundation for how they learn, how they grow, and how they succeed. These educators are central to that process. They do far more than teach. They create safe, engaging environments where children can thrive.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Panetta
featured_quotes.text: By expanding eligibility for the educator expense deduction to early-childhood educators, the bill will finally recognize the incredible dedication and work of these pre-K educators. This is one step toward supporting those who extend themselves day in and day out to help grow and educate all of our children.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: when it comes to supporting teachers who go the extra mile to provide for their students, including paying out of pocket for supplies and other educational materials, we need to ensure we are acknowledging and rewarding the contributions of all of our educators. That includes the early-childhood teachers, who are charged with instilling in our youth a love of learning and curiosity from the youngest age.

gaps: The bill does not define "early childhood educator" or specify which types of early childhood education institutions qualify, leaving scope determination to IRS rulemaking.

The $300 deduction cap — which applies to K-12 teachers and would apply to early childhood educators under this bill — is not adjusted for the early childhood context, where out-of-pocket supply costs may differ from those of K-12 classroom teachers.

modified: Section 62(d)(1)(A) and (B) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 — above-the-line educator expense deduction expanded to include early childhood educators in schools providing pre-kindergarten education

bills.title: BARCODE Efficiency Act
bills.official_title: Barcode Automation for Revenue Collection to Organize Disbursement and Enhance Efficiency Act
bills.summary: When taxpayers prepare their returns electronically but print and mail them, the IRS currently re-enters all that data by hand. This bill requires those returns to include a scannable barcode so the IRS can convert them to electronic format automatically. For returns prepared entirely by hand and for paper correspondence, the IRS must use optical character recognition software. The technology requirement can be waived if the IRS finds it slower or less reliable than manual processing — but any waiver must be reported to Congress within 30 days.
bills.brief: Mandates barcodes on electronically-prepared paper returns and OCR scanning for handwritten returns and correspondence, with a performance-based waiver.

top_lines.headline: Barcode Mandate
subs: Electronically-prepared paper returns must include a scannable barcode — IRS must scan rather than manually re-enter the data
Applies to individual income tax returns 180 days after enactment

top_lines.headline: OCR for Everything Else
subs: Hand-prepared returns and all paper IRS correspondence must be transcribed using optical character recognition
Estate and gift returns: 24 months; all other returns and correspondence: 12 months after enactment

top_lines.headline: Performance Waiver
subs: IRS may skip the technology if it's slower or less reliable than manual processing — but must report to Congress within 30 days

bills.likelihoodReason: Bipartisan sponsorship (Schneider D-IL and Yakym R-IN) and the efficiency framing make opposition difficult to articulate, but only 1 cosponsor. IRS technology mandate bills often face implementation feasibility questions in the Senate, particularly when they include performance-based exceptions that give the agency discretion to delay compliance.

sections.label: Section 2 — Scanning and Digitization of Tax Returns and Correspondence

items.main: Requires that any federal tax return prepared electronically and filed on paper must include a scannable code, and that the IRS must use barcode scanning technology to convert such returns to electronic format.
items.detail: If the barcode data cannot be accurately converted, the IRS must use optical character recognition or functionally similar technology. For paper returns not prepared electronically and all paper correspondence (except correspondence originally received electronically), the IRS must use OCR technology to transcribe the document. Effective dates: individual income tax returns within 180 days; all other returns and correspondence within 12 months; estate and gift tax returns within 24 months of enactment.

items.main: The technology requirement is waived if the Secretary determines it is slower or less reliable than manual transcription or any other IRS process — but a waiver report must be submitted to Congress within 30 days.
items.detail: The waiver determination is made entirely by the Secretary without independent oversight or minimum performance benchmarks. The reporting obligation to the Ways and Means Committee and Senate Finance Committee is the sole check on waiver use.

underreported.summary: The IRS determines whether its own technology is slower or less reliable than manual processing. If it makes that finding, it may waive the barcode and OCR requirements with no congressional approval required — only a 30-day report.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's mandate reads as a firm requirement. The waiver mechanism allows the IRS to indefinitely delay compliance through its own performance assessment, with a notification-only check. No minimum performance threshold, time limit on the waiver, or independent evaluation is specified.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Yakym
featured_quotes.text: I am proud to co-lead this act with my friend from Illinois (Mr. Schneider). This is a simple but powerful bill that will make tax return processing faster, more accurate, and more efficient. E-filing taxes is becoming even more common. In 2009, two-thirds of taxpayers e-filed their returns. By 2015, it was up to 85 percent. Last year, 94 percent of taxpayers e-filed their returns. That remaining 6 percent still accounts for 10 million tax returns. There are good reasons to file a paper return.

gaps: The bill requires OCR for paper correspondence but does not address accuracy standards for the OCR process or what happens when digitized data contains errors that affect tax calculations or processing.

The bill does not specify what recourse taxpayers have if their paper-filed barcode return is misread or if the OCR transcription of their correspondence contains errors that affect their tax account.

added: Requirement for scannable barcodes on electronically-prepared federal tax returns filed in paper format
Requirement for IRS to use barcode scanning technology to convert electronically-prepared paper returns to electronic format
Requirement for IRS to use optical character recognition technology for hand-prepared paper returns and paper correspondence
Performance-based waiver with 30-day congressional reporting requirement

bills.title: To amend title 5, United States Code, to authorize the increase of the retirement age in the United States Capitol Police.
bills.official_title: To amend title 5, United States Code, to authorize the increase of the retirement age in the United States Capitol Police.
bills.summary: Capitol Police officers must currently retire at age 57, though the Capitol Police Board can waive that requirement and allow officers to work until age 60. This bill expands the Board's authority to set the mandatory retirement age at any point between 57 and 65, giving it more flexibility to retain experienced officers beyond the current 60-year cap.
bills.brief: Raises the Capitol Police Board's maximum retirement age waiver from 60 to 65, letting the Board keep experienced officers working longer.

top_lines.headline: Retirement Age Flexibility
subs: Capitol Police Board can now set mandatory retirement at any age between 57 and 65 — up from the current 57–60 range
Applies to officers under both the Civil Service Retirement System and the Federal Employees' Retirement System

bills.likelihoodReason: Bipartisan support (Steil R-WI and Morelle D-NY) on a narrow workforce management bill affecting a single law enforcement agency. Capitol security legislation typically advances with little controversy. The limited scope and lack of broader policy implications make Senate passage plausible if floor time is available.

sections.label: Section 1 — Retirement Age Increase

items.main: Amends Sections 8335(c) and 8425(c) of title 5, United States Code to expand the Capitol Police Board's authority over mandatory retirement age from a fixed ceiling of 60 to a range of 57 to 65.
items.detail: Both the Civil Service Retirement System (Section 8335(c)) and Federal Employees' Retirement System (Section 8425(c)) provisions are amended by replacing "becomes 60 years of age" with "attains an age determined by the Board that shall be not less than 57 years of age and not more than 65 years of age." The minimum mandatory retirement age of 57 is unchanged. The Board retains discretion to set the mandatory retirement age anywhere within the 57–65 range for individual officers or as a general policy.

gaps: The bill grants the Board discretion to set retirement age between 57 and 65 but specifies no criteria the Board must use in making that determination for individual officers or as a department-wide policy.

modified: Section 8335(c) of title 5, United States Code (CSRS) — Capitol Police mandatory retirement age ceiling raised from 60 to 65, at the Board's discretion
Section 8425(c) of title 5, United States Code (FERS) — Capitol Police mandatory retirement age ceiling raised from 60 to 65, at the Board's discretion

bills.title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
bills.official_title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
bills.summary: When customs agents suspect imported goods are counterfeit or pirated, they can already ask brand owners to help identify violations — but only certain information can be shared. This bill expands that program to let CBP share nonpublic data generated by online marketplaces, freight forwarders, and shipping operators with brand owners and any other party the Commissioner determines has an interest in the merchandise. It also broadens the physical evidence that can be shared to include packing materials and shipping containers.
bills.brief: Expands what counterfeit-goods intelligence CBP can share with brand owners — adding marketplace and freight data, packing materials, and a broader circle of eligible recipients.

top_lines.headline: Counterfeit Goods Detection
subs: CBP can now share nonpublic data from online marketplaces, freight forwarders, and express consignment operators with brand owners
Packing materials and shipping containers added to physical evidence that can be shared

top_lines.headline: Broader Access
subs: Any party with an interest in the merchandise may receive the shared information — not just trademark or copyright owners
Sharing threshold raised from "suspects" to "has a reasonable suspicion" of a violation

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship (Moore R-UT and Schneider D-IL) and 6 cosponsors, and anti-counterfeiting measures attract broad support. However, the Senate calendar for narrowly focused trade bills is unpredictable, and the expansion of data-sharing to cover marketplace and freight operator nonpublic information may draw scrutiny over privacy and due process for importers.

sections.label: Section 1 — Expansion of CBP Information Sharing

items.main: Amends Section 628A(a) of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1628a) to authorize CBP to share nonpublic information generated by online marketplaces, express consignment operators, freight forwarders, and other importation-chain entities with parties requesting assistance in identifying IP violations.
items.detail: CBP may provide a requesting party with nonpublic information about suspected infringing merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity involved in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States, provided that information was provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. The scope of shareable physical evidence expands to include packing materials and shipping containers, in addition to the merchandise and its packaging. The threshold for initiating the sharing is raised from "suspects" to "has a reasonable suspicion" that merchandise is being imported in violation of trademark or copyright law.

items.main: Expands the class of parties eligible to receive CBP information to any party with an interest in the merchandise, as determined appropriate by the Commissioner.
items.detail: Current law limits the program to trademark or copyright owners requesting assistance to determine whether merchandise violates their rights. The bill adds a new paragraph (5) to Section 628A(b) allowing the Commissioner to extend access to any other party with an interest in the merchandise. No statutory definition of "interest" or limit on the Commissioner's discretion to determine eligibility is provided.

underreported.summary: The bill extends information sharing to "any other party with an interest in the merchandise, as determined appropriate by the Commissioner." No statutory definition of "interest" is provided, and the Commissioner's authority to determine who qualifies is unconstrained by the bill.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline purpose is expanding anti-counterfeiting tools for brand owners. The open-ended recipient provision in paragraph (5) goes beyond brand owners and trademark holders to any party the Commissioner deems interested — a category that could include competitors of the importer, brokers, or other commercial parties not directly harmed by the alleged violation.

gaps: The bill authorizes sharing of nonpublic information generated by online marketplaces and freight operators but does not specify what categories of nonpublic data are covered or whether any types of data are excluded from the sharing authority.
The bill does not address the rights of the importer or the source entity (e.g., the online marketplace) to receive notice that their nonpublic information has been shared with a third party.

added: Section 628A(a)(3) of the Tariff Act of 1930 — CBP authority to share nonpublic information generated by online marketplaces, express consignment operators, freight forwarders, and other importation-chain entities with parties assisting in IP violation determinations
Section 628A(b)(5) — Commissioner authority to share information with any other party with an interest in the merchandise
modified: Section 628A(a) of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1628a) — sharing threshold changed from "suspects" to "has a reasonable suspicion" of a trademark or copyright violation
Section 628A(a)(1) — physical evidence shareable with requesting parties expanded to include packing materials and shipping containers

bills.title: IRS Whistleblower Program Improvement Act
bills.official_title: IRS Whistleblower Program Improvement Act
bills.summary: The IRS Whistleblower Program pays people who report tax fraud — but when the IRS shortchanges their award, whistleblowers currently face a stacked deck in Tax Court: judges can only overrule the IRS if it acted unreasonably. This bill replaces that with full de novo review where courts examine the evidence fresh. It also lets whistleblowers stay anonymous in court, adds interest to awards when the IRS delays notifying them, requires the IRS to publish the top 10 tax avoidance schemes reported by whistleblowers each year, and extends the attorney fee tax deduction to all whistleblower awards.
bills.brief: Strengthens IRS whistleblower protections: de novo court review of awards, Tax Court anonymity, interest on delayed payments, and expanded attorney fee deductions.

top_lines.headline: De Novo Court Review
subs: Tax Court must now review IRS whistleblower award decisions from scratch — not just for unreasonableness
Applies to petitions already pending on the date of enactment

top_lines.headline: Anonymity and Delays
subs: Whistleblowers may proceed anonymously in Tax Court unless public interest outweighs harm to them
Interest accrues on awards when IRS misses its preliminary recommendation deadline

top_lines.headline: Fees and Reporting
subs: Attorney fee deduction extended to discretionary awards — currently limited to mandatory awards only
IRS annual report must list up to 10 top tax avoidance schemes disclosed by whistleblowers

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship (Kelly R-PA and Thompson D-CA) and 5 cosponsors. Whistleblower protections have broad appeal, but the shift to de novo review is a significant reduction in IRS deference that the Treasury Department is likely to resist in the Senate. The combination of five substantive changes creates multiple points of potential objection.

sections.label: Section 2 — De Novo Review of Award Determinations

items.main: Amends Section 7623(b)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to require the Tax Court to review IRS whistleblower award determinations de novo rather than under the current abuse of discretion standard.
items.detail: Under current law, Tax Court review uses an abuse of discretion standard — the court only overturns the IRS if its determination was unreasonable, giving the agency substantial deference. The amendment requires de novo review based on the administrative record established at the time of the original determination, plus any newly discovered or previously unavailable evidence. The provision heading is changed from "Appeal" to "Review." Applies to petitions pending on or filed after enactment.

sections.label: Section 3 — Whistleblower Anonymity Before the Tax Court

items.main: Adds Section 7623(b)(6)(D) allowing whistleblowers to proceed anonymously in all Tax Court proceedings under the whistleblower program.
items.detail: Tax Court proceedings are generally public under sections 7458 and 7461 of the Internal Revenue Code. This section overrides those provisions for whistleblower cases unless the Tax Court finds that a societal interest in disclosing the whistleblower's identity exceeds the potential harm disclosure could cause to the whistleblower. No definition of "societal interest" is provided. Applies to petitions pending on or filed after enactment.

sections.label: Sections 4–6 — Reporting, Interest, and Attorney Fees

items.main: Requires the IRS annual whistleblower report to include descriptions of up to 10 top tax avoidance schemes disclosed by whistleblowers during the year.
items.detail: Amends Section 406(c) of the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 to add the scheme-listing requirement to the existing annual report. Applies to reports for fiscal years ending after enactment.

items.main: Adds interest on mandatory whistleblower awards when the IRS fails to provide timely preliminary award recommendation notice, and extends the attorney fee tax deduction to discretionary whistleblower awards.
items.detail: Under current law, attorney fees paid in connection with a whistleblower award may be deducted from adjusted gross income only when the award is made through the mandatory program. The bill extends this deduction to fees paid in connection with discretionary awards. Interest accrues at the overpayment rate under the Internal Revenue Code when the IRS fails to meet its preliminary recommendation notice deadline.

underreported.summary: Whistleblowers may proceed anonymously unless the Tax Court finds that a "societal interest" in disclosure outweighs potential harm to the whistleblower. The bill does not define "societal interest."
underreported.why_unreported: The anonymity protection is presented as the default rule. The exception that overrides it — a judicial finding of "societal interest" — uses a term with no statutory definition, leaving the strength of the protection entirely to Tax Court discretion on a case-by-case basis. The operative limit on the anonymity guarantee is therefore undefined.

gaps: The bill changes Tax Court review to de novo but does not set a deadline for Tax Court proceedings after a whistleblower petition is filed, which has historically been a significant source of delay in award resolution.

The bill extends the attorney fee deduction to discretionary awards but does not address the treatment of fees in cases where a whistleblower prevails in Tax Court review but the underlying award amount is subsequently reduced.

added: Section 7623(b)(6)(D) of the Internal Revenue Code — whistleblower anonymity in Tax Court proceedings absent a finding of overriding societal interest
Section 7623(b)(7) — interest on mandatory whistleblower awards when IRS fails to provide timely preliminary award recommendation notice
Requirement for IRS annual whistleblower report to include descriptions of up to 10 top tax avoidance schemes disclosed by whistleblowers
modified: Section 7623(b)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code — Tax Court review of whistleblower award determinations changed from abuse of discretion to de novo, based on the administrative record plus newly discovered evidence
Section 104(a)(2) attorney fee deduction extended from mandatory whistleblower awards to include discretionary whistleblower awards

bills.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to Public Land Order No. 7917 for Withdrawal of Federal Lands; Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, MN.
bills.official_title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to Public Land Order No. 7917 for Withdrawal of Federal Lands; Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, MN.
bills.summary: In 2023, the Bureau of Land Management blocked mineral mining and geothermal drilling on 225,504 acres of National Forest land in Minnesota — including land bordering the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and the 1854 Ceded Territory of the Lake Superior Chippewa — for 20 years to protect the watershed. This joint resolution, signed into law under the Congressional Review Act, cancels that protection and reopens the land for mineral and geothermal leasing.
bills.brief: Cancels the federal mining ban on 225,504 acres of Minnesota National Forest bordering the Boundary Waters, reopening it for mineral and geothermal leasing.

top_lines.headline: Mining Ban Reversed
subs: 225,504 acres of Minnesota National Forest reopened for mineral and geothermal leasing
Nullifies a 2023 BLM order that had barred mining for 20 years

top_lines.headline: What Was Protected
subs: Land borders the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and the 1854 Ceded Territory of the Lake Superior Chippewa

bills.title: Ensuring Children Receive Support Act
bills.official_title: Ensuring Children Receive Support Act
bills.summary: When a parent owes more than $2,500 in unpaid child support, federal law already requires the State Department to deny them a new passport — but revoking an existing passport is currently optional. This bill makes revocation mandatory in those same circumstances, requires the government to notify the individual before acting, and gives the State Department explicit statutory authority to issue a short-term return-home passport for individuals abroad who need to come back to the United States.

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Revocation

sections.label: Section 2 — Passport Revocation for Child Support Arrearage

items.detail: Current law gives the State Department discretion to "revoke, restrict, or limit" a passport in these circumstances. The $2,500 arrearage threshold set by the Office of Child Support Enforcement of the Department of Health and Human Services is unchanged.

items.main: Authorizes the State Department to issue a limited-duration temporary passport solely for return travel to the United States for affected individuals who are abroad in an emergency.

bills.title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
bills.official_title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
bills.summary: Under current tax law, settlement and judgment damages are only tax-free if they stem from a physical injury — and the IRS has interpreted this to require visible harm like bruising or cuts. This bill creates a separate tax exemption for sexual assault and abuse damages that requires no proof of physical injury and no medical records. If a judgment or settlement states that damages result from sexual acts or contact, the IRS must prove otherwise in court rather than the survivor having to prove it.
bills.brief: Creates a tax exemption for sexual assault damages requiring no physical injury proof or medical records, and shifts the burden of proof to the IRS.

top_lines.headline: New Tax Exemption
subs: Sexual assault and abuse damages excluded from gross income — no visible injury or medical records required
Applies to non-punitive damages from judgments and settlements entered after enactment

top_lines.headline: Burden of Proof Shift
subs: IRS must prove damages are not on account of sexual acts if the judgment or agreement says they are
Medical records alone cannot be required to deny the exemption

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill addresses a sympathetic population with bipartisan appeal — sexual assault survivors facing unexpected tax liability — and passed the House. sections.label: Section 2 — Exclusion from Gross Income

items.main: Amends Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude from gross income damages received on account of any sexual act (as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246(2)) or sexual contact (as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246(3)), other than punitive damages.
items.detail: Current law limits the exclusion to damages "on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness." The IRS has interpreted this to require observable bodily harm. The amendment adds sexual acts and sexual contact as an independent basis for the exclusion, removing the physical injury requirement for these claims. The amendment applies to amounts received pursuant to judgments made, and agreements entered into, after the date of enactment.

items.main: New Section 104(d) establishes that damages are substantiated as on account of sexual act or contact if the judgment or agreement so states, and prohibits denying the exclusion solely for lack of medical records.
items.detail: The IRS bears the burden of proving that damages characterized as on account of sexual act or contact in a judgment or agreement are not so characterized, in any related court proceeding. A judgment is treated as made after enactment if the first payment pursuant to it is received after enactment. An agreement that replaces, supersedes, or revises an agreement entered into before enactment does not qualify as a new post-enactment agreement.

items.main: Requires the Secretary of the Treasury to conduct a public awareness program about the new exclusion in consultation with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women.
items.detail: The Secretary must work with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women and other relevant federal agencies to promote public awareness of the exclusion from gross income provided by the new Section 104(a)(2)(B). No timeline, funding level, or required outreach methods are specified in the bill.

underreported.summary: An agreement that replaces, supersedes, or revises a pre-enactment agreement does not qualify as a new post-enactment agreement, even if the replacement is reached after enactment.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is to extend the tax exemption to sexual assault survivors. This provision specifically bars survivors who renegotiate or revise a pre-existing settlement after enactment from accessing the new exemption, a limitation not apparent from the bill's title or the headline exemption provision.

bills.title: Main Street Capital Access Act
bills.likelihoodReason: Rep. Hill (R-AR), Chair of the House Financial Services Committee, sponsored this bill with 33 Republican cosponsors and zero Democratic support — a strictly partisan track. House passage is plausible given the Republican majority, but Senate passage requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, and the complete absence of Democratic cosponsors signals no crossover appeal. The CBLR capital floor reduction and the one-way GDP ratchet will draw organized opposition from consumer protection and banking reform groups, making Senate passage unlikely without significant amendment.

sections.label: Title I — New Bank Formation and Local Community Access

items.main: New rural depository institutions (under $10B total assets) receive a 3-year capital phase-in with CBLR capped at the lesser of the standard rate or 7.5%
items.detail: Rural defined as county outside metropolitan or micropolitan statistical area per OMB Urban Influence Codes, or census block not in urban area per latest Census. Business plan deviations must be approved, conditionally approved, or denied within 30 days — failure to act is deemed approval. items.main: CDFI Bond Guarantee Program annual cap set at $1B with $25M minimum per transaction; guarantee fees range 10–15 basis points; program extended through December 31, 2028
items.detail: Section 106 amends Section 114A, Community Development Banking and Financial Institutions Act of 1994 (12 U.S.C. 4713a). Secretary of Treasury must issue a report to Congress on program effectiveness not later than 3 years after enactment. The Sense of Congress affirms the program furthers the CDFI Fund mission to increase economic opportunity for underserved populations and distressed communities.

items.main: National bank investment threshold in bank premises raised from 15% to 20% in both Section 5136 of the Revised Statutes (12 U.S.C. 24) and Section 9 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 338a)

Section 105 adds a requirement that the CDFI Fund Secretary annually testify before Congressional financial committees at the discretion of committee chairs.

sections.label: Title II — Tailoring Bank Regulation

items.main: Community Bank Leverage Ratio eligibility threshold raised from $10B to $15B; qualifying capital ratio range changed from 8–10% to 6–9%
items.detail: Section 203 amends Section 201, Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act (12 U.S.C. 5371 note). Agencies must propose rule changes within 180 days and finalize within 1 year. Board of Governors, OCC, and FDIC must review the CBLR and report to Congress within 150 days covering opt-in incentives, burden relief, and reporting simplification.

items.main: 47 thresholds across 14 federal statutes adjusted upward for historical GDP growth; all thresholds recalibrated every 5 years beginning April 1, 2031
items.detail: Representative adjustments under Section 205: CRA small bank threshold $250M → $800M; Federal Home Loan Bank membership $1B → $3B; FDIC independent audit threshold $150M → $800M; Depository Institution Management Interlocks Act threshold $100M → $600M; Home Mortgage Disclosure Act small institution threshold $30M → $160M. New Sections 177 and 178 of the Financial Stability Act of 2010 establish the GDP-indexed adjustment mechanism with rounding rules and Federal Register publication by April 5 of each adjustment year.

items.main: Small Bank Holding Company consolidated asset threshold raised to $6B; Board of Governors must revise Appendix C to Part 225, Title 12, Code of Federal Regulations within 180 days
items.detail: Appendix C is commonly known as the Small Bank Holding Company and Savings and Loan Holding Company Policy Statement. The higher threshold reduces holding company-level capital and debt issuance requirements for mid-size regional banks previously above the old threshold.

Applies only to credit unions with CAMELS composite rating of 1 or 2 AND capability of management rating of 1 or 2. sections.label: Title III — Fair and Transparent Bank Supervision

items.main: Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council required to reform CAMELS rating system to use articulable, clear, and reviewable criteria; management component must be either eliminated or limited to objective governance measures

Revised criteria must ensure composite ratings reflect material financial condition and solvency, incorporate compliance with anti-money laundering requirements (Section 21, Federal Deposit Insurance Act; Subchapter II, Chapter 53, Title 31 U.S.C.), and use transparent methodology limited to objective CAMELS component criteria. bills.official_title: A bill to amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Section 702 of FISA lets the NSA collect the communications of foreign targets without a warrant — including conversations involving Americans. This bill is the second short-term extension in as many weeks, stretching that authority from its April 30, 2026 expiration to June 12, 2026 with no new limits or reforms added.
bills.brief: Extends NSA warrantless surveillance authority under FISA Section 702 by six more weeks, to June 12, 2026, with no changes to oversight or limitations.

underreported.section: Section 209 — No TSA Exemptions for Officials
underreported.summary: Members of Congress, Cabinet secretaries, agency heads, and senior White House staff are explicitly barred from exemptions from federal passenger and baggage screening. A separate provision bars future legislation from overriding this requirement using funds from this act.
underreported.why_unreported: Appropriations bills frequently include policy riders that never surface in coverage of the headline funding numbers. This provision directly names elected officials and executive appointees as subject to the same screening requirements as the public.

underreported.summary: CBP is barred from preventing individuals from importing up to a 90-day personal-use supply of prescription drugs from Canada that comply with FDA standards. Controlled substances and biological products are excluded.

underreported.section: Section 204 — No New Border Crossing Fees
underreported.summary: The Secretary of Homeland Security is prohibited from establishing, collecting, or studying any new fee charged to pedestrians, cyclists, or vehicle occupants crossing the Southern or Northern border at a land port of entry.
underreported.why_unreported: Border crossing fees have been discussed as a potential revenue mechanism. This provision explicitly blocks even a feasibility study, making it a quiet but firm policy prohibition embedded in the appropriations text.

bills.title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
bills.summary: Under current law, gasoline blended with 15% ethanol (E15) cannot be sold at gas stations during summer months because E15 evaporates more readily than E10, contributing to ground-level ozone. This bill removes that summer ban by extending the existing E10 vapor pressure waiver to cover E15 year-round, allowing gas stations in all states to sell E15 from June 1 through September 15.
bills.brief: Allows E15 ethanol-blended gasoline to be sold year-round by extending the E10 Reid Vapor Pressure waiver to E15, removing the current summer ozone-season prohibition.

top_lines.headline: Ethanol Blend Waiver
subs: Applies the existing Clean Air Act Reid Vapor Pressure waiver for E10 to gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol
Removes the current June 1–September 15 prohibition on E15 sales that applies in most of the country

top_lines.headline: Who It Affects
subs: Fuel retailers who currently stock separate summer and year-round fuel blends would be able to carry E15 year-round
Consumers in corn-belt states where E15 is already common would no longer face seasonal supply interruptions

bills.likelihoodReason: Passed the House with 54 bipartisan cosponsors, signaling strong rural-state support. The Senate has passed similar measures before. However, opposition from oil refiners and some environmental groups over ozone concerns remains, and no Senate companion bill has advanced. Senate leadership is currently focused on the budget reconciliation process, limiting floor time for standalone bills.

sections.label: Section 1 — Ethanol Waiver Extension

items.main: Amends Section 211(h) of the Clean Air Act to extend the Reid Vapor Pressure waiver that currently applies to gasoline with 10% ethanol to gasoline blended with any percentage of ethanol up to 15%.
items.detail: Reid Vapor Pressure measures how readily gasoline evaporates; higher RVP fuel contributes to ground-level ozone formation in warm weather. The Clean Air Act currently caps summer RVP at 9.0 psi in most areas but waives that limit for E10. This bill extends the waiver to E15, allowing it to be sold at the same locations that carry E10 without requiring separate summer and winter fuel inventories.

underreported.summary: The RVP waiver extension applies to all ethanol blend percentages from 10% up to 15%, not just to E15 specifically. A retailer blending at 12% or 13% ethanol would also fall under the waiver.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title and sponsor statements focus on E15, but the statutory amendment covers any blend up to 15%, meaning mid-range blends sold during the summer ozone season would also be exempt from the 9.0 psi RVP cap.

gaps: The bill removes the summer RVP restriction on E15 but does not address the separate infrastructure requirements — many fuel pumps and storage tanks require upgrades to handle E15 — that limit its availability regardless of the waiver.
The bill extends the waiver nationally but does not address California, which operates under a separate state waiver system and would require additional EPA approval to participate.

sections.label: Title III — Bilateral Economic Assistance

sections.label: Title IV — International Security Assistance

sections.label: Section 101 — Funding Limitation

sections.label: Sections 101–105 — CR Extension and Ratification

items.detail: Sec. 101: amends date in Sec. 106(3) of Public Law 119-37 to February 13, 2026. Sec. 102: lapse period treated as covered by the CR. Sec. 103: personnel pay authorized under 31 U.S.C. § 1341(c). Sec. 104: obligations for essential activity and orderly termination ratified. Sec. 105: repeals Section 213 of the prior CR affecting legislative branch operations.

sections.label: Sections 5001–5003 — Agriculture and Commodity Extenders

sections.label: Sections 5004–5009 — Homeland Security and Cybersecurity Extenders

sections.label: Sections 5010–5018 — Government Operations and Justice Extenders

sections.label: Title I — Medicaid

sections.label: Title II — Medicare

items.main: Extends low-volume hospital payments, Medicare-Dependent Hospital program, ambulance add-ons, APM incentives, telehealth, and hospital-at-home; adds MCED screening and infusion pump coverage; and increases the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.403B to $2.062B.
items.detail: Telehealth (Sec. 6209) continues COVID-19 era flexibilities. Acute Hospital Care at Home (Sec. 6210) extends CMS waiver for hospital-level home care. MCED (Sec. 6221) amends Section 1861 of the Social Security Act. PBM accountability (Sec. 6224): fiduciary requirements and spread pricing restrictions for Part D PBMs.

sections.label: Title III — Human Services

items.main: Extends TANF through December 31, 2026 (Sec. 6304), sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education programs (Secs. 6301-6302), and family-to-family health information centers (Sec. 6303).
items.detail: TANF extension: 'such sums as may be necessary' appropriation language; continues FY2025 program terms. Sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education extended under the same mechanism — no new conditions added.

sections.label: Title IV — Public Health and Other Extenders

items.main: Extends community health centers, NHSC, and teaching health center GME programs (Sec. 6401); Special Diabetes Programs at $350M for FY2026 (Sec. 6402); and appropriates $188M for No Surprises Act implementation (Sec. 6404).
items.detail: Community health centers: continued funding through extension period. Special Diabetes Programs: $350M for type 1 and type 2 programs. No Surprises Act (Sec. 6404): $188M to CMS Program Management Account, available until expended, for independent dispute resolution and consumer protection administration.

sections.label: Title VI — Food and Drug Administration

items.main: Extends rare pediatric disease priority review vouchers (Sec. 6604), modifies orphan drug exclusivity (Sec. 6605), and establishes an Abraham Accords Office within the FDA (Sec. 6611).
items.detail: Sec. 6604: rare pediatric disease voucher program extended. Sec. 6605: limits 30-month orphan drug exclusivity to prevent dual-use abuse. Sec. 6611: new FDA office for Abraham Accords implementation including regulatory cooperation with Israel and signatory states on pharmaceutical approvals.

sections.label: Title VII — Lowering Prescription Drug Costs

items.main: Adds PBM oversight requirements (Sec. 6701), remittance transparency rules (Sec. 6702), and generic drug application transparency (Sec. 6703).
items.detail: Sec. 6701: PBMs providing Medicare Part D services must comply with new reporting and oversight requirements. Sec. 6702: PBM remittance and pass-through structures in drug pricing made transparent. Sec. 6703: generic drug application transparency reduces barriers to market entry.

criticisms.why: This amendment would completely eliminate funding for an office that helps some of the most vulnerable in our country. This office helps shelter and care for children who are seeking safety. It makes sure that these children aren't being trafficked. It makes sure these children aren't stuck in cages in Border Patrol facilities for extended periods of time.

This amendment would eliminate HHS funding provided in the bill — which the Trump administration actually requested in their budget — that will allow the Agency to drastically improve sponsor vetting for unaccompanied children, ensuring that they are no longer released to human traffickers.

gaps: The bill funds five of twelve FY2026 appropriations packages but does not include Agriculture, Commerce/Justice/Science, Energy/Water, Interior/Environment, full-year Homeland Security, or the Legislative Branch.
The DHS continuing resolution runs only through February 13, 2026, leaving border security and immigration enforcement funding unresolved within days of enactment.
Division G bars UNRWA contributions but does not specify alternative humanitarian delivery mechanisms for Palestinian refugees who rely on UNRWA for food, education, and health services.

sections.label: Title V — Independent Agencies

items.main: Funds the SBA's loan guarantee programs ($35.5B 7(a), $15B disaster, $6B SBIC debentures), the General Services Administration, OPM, SEC, and other independent agencies.
items.detail: GSA Federal Buildings Fund: $9.69B installment purchases, $5.57B rental, $3.01B building operations. SBA administrative expenses within Title V. SEC operations primarily offset by transaction fees under the Securities Exchange Act.

underreported.section: IRS Enforcement vs. Taxpayer Services Funding Split
underreported.summary: The IRS Enforcement account ($5.00B) is funded at 64% more than the Taxpayer Services account ($3.04B), with the combined $11.47B appearing across three separate accounts none of which shows the total IRS appropriation.
underreported.why_unreported: The three IRS accounts appear as separate appropriations headings; the relative weight between enforcement and taxpayer services is not visible from any single appropriations line.

underreported.summary: The CFIUS fund is appropriated at $21M but simultaneously reduced to $0 as filing fee collections are received; if collections fall short of $21M, Treasury must absorb the shortfall.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision appears to appropriate $21M but the offset mechanism makes the net general fund cost $0 under the assumption of full fee recovery — an assumption not guaranteed in the bill text.

gaps: Division funds Treasury operations but does not address the statutory debt limit ceiling, which requires separate legislative action.
SBA disaster loan ceiling of $15B provides no emergency supplemental authority for declared disasters occurring after enactment.

underreported.why_unreported: Embedded in general provisions as a transfer authority, the provision allows $850M to be moved away from its appropriated purpose without separate authorization for each reallocation or a defined criteria for 'America First' projects.

underreported.summary: Permanently rescinds $900M from prior-year State and Foreign Operations appropriations previously enacted by Congress.
underreported.why_unreported: A rescission of previously enacted foreign assistance appears as a general provision in Title VII, reducing total foreign assistance authority by $900M beyond the headline appropriation levels without listing the specific accounts affected.

gaps: SEED Act assistance provides $6.77B with a 15% Ukraine minimum but specifies no floor for direct Ukrainian government budget support, leaving distribution to State Department discretion.
FMF designates $3.3B in grants for Israel but provides no equivalent minimum floor for any other ally or partner country beyond Jordan and Egypt.

underreported.section: Sec. 5012 — Sex Offense Special Assessment Made Permanent
underreported.summary: Section 3014(a) of title 18 is amended to remove the September 30, 2025 expiration date from the special assessment on nonindigent persons convicted of federal sex offenses and human trafficking — converting it to a permanent statutory fee with no future reauthorization required.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision is drafted as a deletion of a termination clause rather than a new program creation. Its effect — making a previously temporary assessment permanent — is not indicated in the section heading.

underreported.section: Sec. 5021 — PAYGO Exemption Covers All Division J Health Spending
underreported.summary: Exempts all budgetary costs of Divisions I and J from PAYGO — covering the Medicare Improvement Fund increase, new MCED coverage, TANF extension, and all health extender spending — without requiring any offsetting savings.
underreported.why_unreported: Located in Division I, this provision determines the fiscal treatment of all Division J spending. Readers reviewing Division J health extenders find no indication that the costs require no budget offsets — the disclosure appears only in Division I.

divisions.brief: Adds Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early detection tests, extends telehealth and dozens of expiring Medicare payment policies, increases the Medicare Improvement Fund by $659M, and creates an FDA office for Abraham Accords implementation.

sections.label: Title I — Medicaid

items.main: Streamlines multi-state provider enrollment (Sec. 6101), removes age restrictions for working disabled adults (Sec. 6102), standardizes military family Medicaid coverage (Sec. 6103), and modifies DSH allotments (Secs. 6105-6106).
items.detail: Sec. 6101: out-of-state providers use streamlined enrollment without duplicating in-state requirements. Sec. 6102: removes age cap for working adults with disabilities. Sec. 6103: military relocation cannot cause Medicaid coverage loss. DSH modifications in Secs. 6105-6106 adjust hospital payment calculations.

sections.label: Title II — Medicare

items.main: Extends low-volume hospital payments, Medicare-Dependent Hospital program, ambulance add-ons, APM incentives, telehealth, and hospital-at-home; adds MCED screening and infusion pump coverage; and increases the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.403B to $2.062B.
items.detail: Telehealth (Sec. 6209) continues COVID-19 era flexibilities. Acute Hospital Care at Home (Sec. 6210) extends CMS waiver for hospital-level home care. MCED (Sec. 6221) amends Section 1861 of the Social Security Act. PBM accountability (Sec. 6224): fiduciary requirements and spread pricing restrictions for Part D PBMs.

sections.label: Title III — Human Services

items.main: Extends TANF through December 31, 2026 (Sec. 6304), sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education programs (Secs. 6301-6302), and family-to-family health information centers (Sec. 6303).
items.detail: TANF extension: 'such sums as may be necessary' appropriation language; continues FY2025 program terms. Sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education extended under the same mechanism — no new conditions added.

sections.label: Title IV — Public Health and Other Extenders

items.main: Extends community health centers, NHSC, and teaching health center GME programs (Sec. 6401); Special Diabetes Programs at $350M for FY2026 (Sec. 6402); and appropriates $188M for No Surprises Act implementation (Sec. 6404).
items.detail: Community health centers: continued funding through extension period. Special Diabetes Programs: $350M for type 1 and type 2 programs. No Surprises Act (Sec. 6404): $188M to CMS Program Management Account, available until expended, for independent dispute resolution and consumer protection administration.

sections.label: Title VI — Food and Drug Administration

items.main: Extends rare pediatric disease priority review vouchers (Sec. 6604), modifies orphan drug exclusivity (Sec. 6605), and establishes an Abraham Accords Office within the FDA (Sec. 6611).
items.detail: Sec. 6604: rare pediatric disease voucher program extended. Sec. 6605: limits 30-month orphan drug exclusivity to prevent dual-use abuse. Sec. 6611: new FDA office for Abraham Accords implementation including regulatory cooperation with Israel and signatory states on pharmaceutical approvals.

sections.label: Title VII — Lowering Prescription Drug Costs

items.main: Adds PBM oversight requirements (Sec. 6701), remittance transparency rules (Sec. 6702), and generic drug application transparency (Sec. 6703).
items.detail: Sec. 6701: PBMs providing Medicare Part D services must comply with new reporting and oversight requirements. Sec. 6702: PBM remittance and pass-through structures in drug pricing made transparent. Sec. 6703: generic drug application transparency reduces barriers to market entry.

underreported.section: Sec. 6611 — Abraham Accords Office within FDA
underreported.summary: Creates a permanent new office within the Food and Drug Administration designated specifically for implementing the Abraham Accords — diplomatic normalization agreements between Israel and Arab states — including pharmaceutical regulatory cooperation.
underreported.why_unreported: The FDA is a public health regulatory agency; creating an office within it for diplomatic implementation of a foreign policy agreement is a novel use of the agency's structure. The section appears in a Title VI FDA heading alongside drug review provisions with no indication of its diplomatic function.

underreported.summary: Modifies cost-sharing reduction schedules for low-income Medicare Part D beneficiaries, adjusting subsidy amounts originally established by the Inflation Reduction Act's drug pricing provisions.
underreported.why_unreported: Titled as an 'adjustment,' the provision modifies IRA-created Part D subsidy schedules for low-income enrollees. The connection to the Inflation Reduction Act's drug pricing architecture is not indicated in the section title.

underreported.section: Sec. 5021 (Division I) — PAYGO Exemption Covers All Division J Costs
underreported.summary: All new Medicare and Medicaid spending in Division J is exempted from PAYGO offset requirements by Sec. 5021 of Division I — meaning the Medicare Improvement Fund increase, MCED coverage, and all other health extender costs require no offsets.
underreported.why_unreported: The exemption is in Division I. Readers reviewing Division J health extenders find no indication in Division J that the costs require no budget offsets — the disclosure appears only in the prior division.

PBM accountability requirements (Sec. 6224) apply to Medicare Part D PBMs but do not address commercial insurance or Medicaid PBMs, which operate under separate regulatory frameworks.

bills.title: FIRE Act
bills.official_title: Fire Improvement and Reforming Exceptional Events Act
bills.summary: Under current Clean Air Act rules, states must go through a lengthy EPA review to exclude air quality data influenced by wildfires when calculating NAAQS violations — a process that can take years and leave communities penalized for pollution they did not cause. This bill requires EPA to revise those regulations to create a faster, standardized process for wildfire-influenced data exclusions, and to recognize pre-fire risk reduction activities like prescribed burns as qualifying exceptional events.
bills.brief: Requires EPA to revise its Clean Air Act exceptional events rules to create faster wildfire smoke data exclusions and recognize prescribed burns, protecting communities from being penalized for air quality violations caused by wildfires or wildfire mitigation.

top_lines.headline: Exceptional Events Revision
subs: Requires EPA to revise its exceptional events regulations to include air quality data influenced by wildfire smoke or wildfire mitigation activities
EPA must establish standardized criteria and shorter review timelines for state exceptional event demonstration submissions

top_lines.headline: Pre-Fire Mitigation Recognition
subs: Requires EPA to recognize prescribed burns and other pre-fire risk reduction activities as qualifying exceptional events
States conducting proactive wildfire mitigation would be able to seek data exclusions for the resulting air quality impacts

bills.likelihoodReason: Passed the House and was referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works. The bill has bipartisan appeal in Western wildfire states and eases regulatory compliance burdens without weakening NAAQS standards, generating little opposition. However, with only 3 cosponsors and no Senate companion, floor scheduling depends on committee leadership priorities. The reconciliation-dominated Senate calendar leaves limited bandwidth for standalone environmental bills.

sections.label: Section 2 — Exceptional Events Regulatory Revision

items.main: Requires EPA to revise 40 C.F.R. Part 50 regulations governing exceptional events to address air quality monitoring data influenced by exceptional events or actions to mitigate wildfire risk.
items.detail: Revised regulations must include defined standards for qualifying exceptional events related to wildfire activity, timelines for EPA review of state demonstration submissions, and requirements that qualifying data be excluded from use in NAAQS exceedance and violation determinations.

sections.label: Section 3 — Pre-Fire Mitigation Activities

items.main: Requires EPA regulations to recognize actions taken to mitigate wildfire risk — such as prescribed burns and vegetation management — as qualifying exceptional events.
items.detail: States and tribes conducting prescribed fire or mechanical fuel reduction treatments would be able to file exceptional event demonstrations for air quality data collected during those activities, protecting them from NAAQS violation findings caused by their own mitigation work.

underreported.summary: The revision requirement applies to all exceptional events as defined under Section 319(b) of the Clean Air Act, which includes high wind dust events, stratospheric ozone intrusions, and other natural conditions — not only wildfire smoke.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title and sponsor focus entirely on wildfire smoke, but the regulatory revision mandate covers the full existing exceptional events definition. EPA regulatory changes made in response to this bill would affect the processing of all exceptional event types.

criticisms.why: I rise today in strong opposition to the FIRE Act, a bill that undermines the protections that keeps our air safe to breathe. In 1970, Democrats and Republicans came together to pass the Clean Air Act and put public health at the center of our national policymaking. That was a promise to the American people, and it is a promise we cannot forget. That law has delivered cleaner air and longer lives, but our work is not finished. More than 100 million Americans live in counties with unhealthy levels of pollution.

I stand here in strong opposition to H.R. 6387, the FIRE Act, but more importantly, I rise in fierce defense of the environmental laws that protect our people and our planet. Because on Earth Day, instead of celebrating progress, we are watching a coordinated effort to dismantle the very safeguards that generations of Americans, Democrats and Republicans, have put in place.

I completely understand that many State and local governments are dealing with severe air pollution related to wildfires, but as we approach Earth Day, it is important for us to recognize that efforts like the Clean Air Act should be continued to be implemented to the fullest and even enhanced where necessary. I will be crystal clear: The Clean Air Act already allows States to submit data for air pollution caused by exceptional events, preventing these emissions from penalizing them when determining compliance with air quality standards.

gaps: The bill requires EPA to revise its regulations but sets no deadline by which the revised regulations must be finalized or take effect.
The bill addresses the data exclusion process but does not provide additional resources for EPA to process the increased volume of state demonstration submissions that faster timelines would require.
